The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
  </details>

- **[Analyzing Atypical Local Features in Museum Artifacts using Generative Image Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28549)**  `arXiv:2611.28549`  
  _Maho Kinoshita, Wakana Kuwata, Ryota Mibayashi, Hiroaki Ohshima_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This study proposes a method for analyzing local visual features in museum artifacts that may appear atypical or unexpected. Objects in the same category often share a similar overall shape, while local details such as patterns, decorations, and facial expressions may reflect regional or cultural characteristics. We use the appearance distribution learned by an image generation model as a reference for what is generally expected within an artifact category. For each target region, we exclude images from that region and fine-tune a generative model using only images from the remaining regions. We then mask selected parts of artifact images from the target region and ask the region-excluded model to complete them. If the completed result differs greatly from the original image, the masked part may contain features that are difficult to predict from the appearance learned from other regions. We measure this difference using LPIPS and treat it as reconstruction difficulty for the generative model. We conduct experiments on images of kokeshi dolls, drums, and masks from the collection of the National Museum of Ethnology. For each category, we select several target regions, build region-excluded LoRA models, and perform inpainting on predefined local parts. The results show that typical shapes and simple decorations are often reconstructed consistently, whereas some region-specific colors, patterns, cord arrangements, and painted details are replaced with more common appearances. These results suggest that region-excluded inpainting can serve as an exploratory tool for finding region-specific local visual features in museum artifact images.
  </details>

- **[Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch Learning for LiDAR Anomalous Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28545)**  `arXiv:2611.28545`  
  _Guanyu Jiang, Junjie Cao, Jinshan Pan, Zhixun Su_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Detecting unexpected objects is essential for autonomous driving safety. Most existing LiDAR anomaly detectors rely on semantic discrimination, which primarily captures category-discriminative features but may overlook deviations from broader feature relationships in normal scenes. Reconstruction offers a complementary perspective by assessing consistency with learned normal patterns. However, pointwise reconstruction errors alone struggle to distinguish anomalies from normal variability in complex outdoor point clouds. We propose Structured Residual Reasoning (SRR) to extract additional anomaly evidence from residual structure across feature channels, time sequences, and geometric space. We further establish that semantic discrimination and normal-pattern reconstruction capture fundamentally different yet complementary anomaly evidence: category compatibility and consistency with learned normal patterns, respectively. At matched background false-positive rates, SRR recovers more objects missed entirely by the semantic branch while producing fewer false positives in normal-only scenes. Building on this finding, we propose Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch (RGDB) learning, in which SRR-derived normal-pattern consistency cues guide a semantic-conditioned anomaly decoder to complement reconstruction-based predictions during training. At inference, the two branches jointly exploit their complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments show that standalone SRR establishes a strong reconstruction-based baseline without semantic labels from the target-scene training data, while RGDB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the STU validation set.
  </details>

- **[Centerline-Guided Multi-Class Road Surface Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28544)**  `arXiv:2611.28544`  
  _Xu Ouyang, Lin Gan, Di Ma, Sonnie Chen, Sanjay Boddhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Road-surface extraction from satellite imagery supports geo- graphic mapping, but a binary mask leaves road axes, transverse extent, and junction structure implicit. Learning these proper- ties together is challenging because narrow corridors, merging roads, and occlusions require different geometric cues. We present a centerline-guided multi-class segmentation framework that makes these dependencies explicit. A hierarchical encoder sup- plies shared features, while predicted centerline features and soft probabilities condition specialized regular, intersection, and over- pass decoders. A two-component width branch supplies transverse geometry to regular-surface decoding, and learned feature fusion produces the complete road mask. Unlike independent prediction heads or a fixed union of component masks, this design exchanges geometric information during decoding while retaining separately inspectable outputs. Evaluation of the four-semantic-output con- figuration on CHN6-CUG achieves 65.53% complete-surface IoU, improving on a binary SegFormer-B4 baseline by 1.01 percentage points and reducing false-positive pixels by 11.94%. The results support geometry-aware surface refinement and a richer raster representation for road-map inspection.
  </details>

- **[Where the Image Sits: Vision-Text Order Bias in Jev](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28535)**  `arXiv:2611.28535`  
  _Youzhi Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Jev-style system-1 decision models read a choice from a single prefill. They restrict the next-token distribution to the supplied option labels and return a distribution over the options, with no generation and no parsing. Recent work shows that generative vision-language models are sensitive to the relative order of image and text tokens. We ask whether that sensitivity reaches this Jev-style readout. The answer is always read at the end of the prompt, so moving the image changes the distance from the visual evidence to the decision, but never the position at which the decision is read. Using four placements---prefix, pre-question, pre-options, and suffix---and holding the option listing fixed, we measure argmax flips, total variation, accuracy, calibration, and label marginals. Suffix placement flips 41.0% of decisions and lowers accuracy by 18.6 points. Averaged over the four slots, the curve is monotone, not U-shaped. That shape differs from prior results on generative vision-language models. The effect survives a battery of controls. We also introduce prefix--question averaging (P+Q), a two-forward readout that averages the prefix and pre-question distributions. It is at least as accurate as prefix and outperforms the prior baselines. Our code and data are publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[VG3R: Video Generation Model for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28520)**  `arXiv:2611.28520`  
  _Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Lin Lian, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28489)**  `arXiv:2611.28489`  
  _Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
  </details>

- **[VICA: Video Contextual Agreement for AIGC Video Detection and Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28485)**  `arXiv:2611.28485`  
  _Runheng Lin, Jialiang Shen, Jiyang Zheng, Ruiqi Liu, Zonglin He, Yu Yao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.
  </details>

- **[CAMA: Calibrated Anti-Collapse Marginal Alignment for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28461)**  `arXiv:2611.28461`  
  _Jinho Kang, Yunhui Guo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking.In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.
  </details>

- **[Decoding Frozen Vision Representations for Training-Free Few-Shot Pineapple Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28442)**  `arXiv:2611.28442`  
  _Manfred Gonzalez-Hernandez, Danny Xie-Li, Fabian Fallas-Moya, Camile Lendering, Joaquín Figueira, Erkut Akdag, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Few-shot object detection in agricultural imagery is hampered by dense vegetation, repeated patterns, and scarce annotations. We present a training-free detector that turns dense features from frozen visual foundation models directly into detections, without fine-tuning, a learned head, or external proposals: a whitened foreground-background direction estimated from annotated support images scores every query patch, and the score field is decoded with an adaptive threshold and support-derived geometry. We also test whether predicted relative depth can be fed directly to RGB-pretrained frozen encoders. On aerial pineapple imagery, the detector outperforms PET-DINO and GeCo2 at every evaluated support size; at K=40, predicted depth alone reaches 92% of the RGB performance with DINOv2, and RGB-depth fusion lowers counting error for both encoders. We release the Pineapple Plantation dataset (4,908 aerial frames, 1,995 annotated with 17,609 boxes, predicted depth, leakage-aware splits) and analyse transfer to two further agricultural datasets.
  </details>

- **[Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28419)**  `arXiv:2611.28419`  
  _Mohammad Mahdi Abootorabi, Parvin Mousavi, Purang Abolmaesumi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.
  </details>

- **[Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28402)**  `arXiv:2611.28402`  
  _Yixuan Luo, Yanjing Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
  </details>

- **[TOGO: Take One Image Editor, Get One Video Editor for Free](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28397)**  `arXiv:2611.28397`  
  _Yixuan Luo, Jose Caballero, Yanjing Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. - **[Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28350)**  `arXiv:2611.28350`  
  _Yihao Wu, Runjia Zeng, Tongyan Wang, Renzhong Huang, Chongzhou Fang, Qifan Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28336)**  `arXiv:2611.28336`  
  _Charles Weng, Alexander Martin, Sandra Arcos-Holzinger, Andrew Yates, Dixin Zheng, Yue Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.
  </details>

- **[GlaucomaMarker - Biomarker-Grounded Glaucoma Vision-Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28332)**  `arXiv:2611.28332`  
  _Ahammed Sakir Nabil, Sadia Siraz, Nikita Chincholkar, Atalie C. Thompson, Jason Xiao, Theodore Leng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. In the current clinical setting, glaucoma diagnosis is generally conducted by assessing optic disc cupping and asymmetry. Vision-language models (VLMs) have been utilized in recent years for glaucoma, mostly trained on fixed templates or AI-generated captions, as no public text describes the biomarkers. Our proposed framework, GlaucomaMarker, hypothesizes that retinal structural biomarkers can ground glaucoma-based VLMs. It converts public segmentation masks into sentences describing eleven biomarkers, to teach retinal foundation models to read them. We applied this framework to RETFound (GlaucomaMarker-R) and FLAIR (GlaucomaMarker-F), training on 9,778 images that yielded 45,190 image-text pairs. On a real-world clinical cohort, GlaucomaMarker-F detects glaucoma with an AUROC of 0.905, against 0.848 for FLAIR, and both read the biomarkers where baselines stay near random guessing. Since the biomarker text is computed from existing masks, it comes at no extra cost.
  </details>

- **[Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28321)**  `arXiv:2611.28321`  
  _Amani Aifi, Wassim Bouachir, Ahmed Zgaren, Nizar Bouguila_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available atthis http URL.
  </details>

- **[Task-Agnostic Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection via Prompt Augmentation and Distribution-Aware Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28291)**  `arXiv:2611.28291`  
  _Yonghan Jiang, Zhengyuan Xie, Wenchu Liu, Linlan Huang, Fei Yang, Xialei Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (IVLOD) empowers pre-trained open-vocabulary detectors to continuously learn new visual concepts from sequential tasks without forgetting foundational knowledge. However, existing methods predominantly rely on oracle task identities during inference, severely limiting their open-world practicality. In this paper, we formalize Task-Agnostic IVLOD (TA-IVLOD), a more realistic setting where such priors are unavailable, requiring the model to simultaneously recognize classes from all learned tasks. This unconstrained setting exposes severe performance degradation due to cross-task semantic interference and parameter conflicts. To tackle these challenges, we propose TADA, a novel modular framework. Specifically, TADA introduces Stochastic Prompt Augmentation to mitigate semantic interference via training-time noise injection, and Test-Time Distribution-Aware Fusion to dynamically weight class-specific LoRA experts, effectively resolving parameter conflicts. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines in standard IVLOD and yields substantial improvements in the rigorous TA-IVLOD setting on the ODinW-13 benchmark, while effectively preserving zero-shot generalization on the MS COCO dataset. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28287)**  `arXiv:2611.28287`  
  _Charles Weng, Zixi Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.
  </details>

- **[HandXFM: Semantic-Structural Distillation for Hand Radiograph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28283)**  `arXiv:2611.28283`  
  _Yuxi Long, Ganlin Feng, Lianghong Chen, Liam J. O'Neil, Carol A. Hitchon, Pingzhao Hu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hand radiographs support diverse clinical tasks, including skeletal maturity assessment, rheumatoid arthritis scoring, abnormality screening, and anatomical localization, yet existing models are typically trained separately for each task and dataset. We present HandXFM, a domain-specific foundation model that leverages cross-modality knowledge for comprehensive hand X-ray understanding. HandXFM distills semantic priors from BiomedCLIP and structural cues from a chest X-ray Vision Transformer (ViT) through a unified alignment framework, integrating complementary medical knowledge in an interpretable way. After pretraining, HandXFM can be adapted to a range of musculoskeletal tasks, including bone age estimation, SvH score prediction, abnormality detection, joint localization, bone segmentation, and visual question answering. It consistently outperforms task-specific and single-expert baselines, achieving up to 0.11 improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) for bone age prediction and a 12\% accuracy gain in abnormality classification. Moreover, HandXFM generalizes to unseen datasets and yields cross-attention maps linking clinical terms to anatomical regions. These results demonstrate that multi-expert distillation effectively unifies semantic and structural supervision within a single pretrained model, establishing HandXFM as an interpretable and generalizable foundation model for hand radiograph analysis.
  </details>

- **[Learning a Rule Bank to Revise 3D CT Reports with Independent Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28281)**  `arXiv:2611.28281`  
  _Renjie Liang, Mengxian Lyu, Zijian Xu, Boxin Zhao, Yang Yang, Jinqian Pan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision--language models can generate fluent radiology reports from 3D chest CT scans, yet they may still omit abnormalities or misstate findings. Independent image analysis using models separate from the report model provides additional observations, but acting on uncertain evidence may introduce new errors. We propose an agent system that learns a revision policy represented as an executable rule bank for each report model. Inspired by experience banks, the agent proposes and refines rules using revision outcomes across development cases. During inference, the retained rules guide local edits using independent classifier predictions and quantitative image measurements without retraining the report model. Unedited sentences are preserved, and each change is linked to the rule that triggered it. On CT-RATE, revision increases CE-F1 by 11.5 points for SelfCue-KD and 0.9 points for NV-Reason-CT, with gains across five draft-sampling seeds. SelfCue-KD's CT-FineBench score also increases by 15.2 points. Draft-only rule learning yields limited gains, while the two image-evidence sources provide complementary benefits for abnormality detection. Measurements also supply numerical details missing from the drafts. These results support learning model-specific rules to control how independent image evidence informs report revision. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[eSPG: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Event Speckle Plethysmography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28275)**  `arXiv:2611.28275`  
  _Aniket Dashpute, Anirudh Bindiganavale Harish, Bhargav Ghanekar, Alankar Kotwal, Andrew Negrut, Syna Gupta, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Non-contact measurement of vital signs such as heart rate (HR) is valuable for patient monitoring and rescue operations. However, existing methods struggle with ambient illumination and motion, and have been demonstrated only at distances of tens of meters. Here we introduce event speckle plethysmography (eSPG), which illuminates a body part with a low-power (0.5-5 mW) laser and captures the resulting dynamic speckle pattern using an event camera. Event cameras, with their high dynamic range, temporal resolution, and sensitivity to intensity changes, are well-suited to capturing rapid speckle fluctuations that encode the physiological signal, even under challenging illumination and imaging conditions. We demonstrate HR estimation at 1 km with a mean absolute error of 5 beats per minute, and 90% of estimates satisfy an AAMI-defined HR estimation criterion. This distance exceeds previous remote plethysmography demonstrations by an order of magnitude and previous speckle plethysmography demonstrations by over three orders of magnitude. We also study and characterize robustness to motion and ambient illumination. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that resolving dynamic speckle fluctuations enables accurate heart rate estimation even at kilometer-scale distances, establishing a new direction toward robust, non-contact physiological monitoring.
  </details>

- **[DeFlowCritic: Dense Latent Reward Alignment for Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28265)**  `arXiv:2611.28265`  
  _Zeeshan Khan, Xin Yu, Shizhe Chen, Cordelia Schmid_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Online reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for aligning text-to-image flow matching models with complex user intent. However, existing methods typically rely on sparse rewards computed only from final decoded images. This delays credit assignment across the denoising trajectory and makes training computationally expensive. Moreover, simply combining multiple rewards does not reliably produce a Pareto trade-off, where gains in compositional accuracy often degrade aesthetic quality. In this work, we propose DeFlowCritic, an efficient online RL framework based on Dense Latent Reward Alignment. Unlike prior work, our method provides dense supervision on intermediate latents, enabling early-stage guidance for the denoising trajectory. To achieve this, we introduce an internal critic that evaluates noisy latents using features extracted directly from the diffusion model, a representation inherently better suited for latent-space reward estimation than standard image encoders. We construct a high-quality reward-modeling dataset with continuous scores for critic training, capturing compositional correctness on high-quality reference images. The resulting dense reward enables efficient online RL training and inference-time scaling. Experiments show that our method achieves a superior balance between prompt faithfulness and visual quality on GenEval2 and T2I-CompBench++ benchmarks. The approach also generalizes across text-to-image flow matching models, including SD3.5-Medium, SD3.5-Large, and FLUX.1-dev.
  </details>

- **[A Closed-Form Temporal Readout for Surgical Triplet Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28240)**  `arXiv:2611.28240`  
  _Lemar Abdi, Amaan Valiuddin, Fida Mohammad Thoker, Karen Sanchez, Bernard Ghanem, Fons van der Sommen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
  </details>

- **[Video-as-Weights: Compiling a Video Once into Parametric and Token Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28221)**  `arXiv:2611.28221`  
  _Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap.To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths.Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
  </details>

- **[FastD4RT: Training-Free Acceleration of Dynamic 4D Reconstruction and Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28193)**  `arXiv:2611.28193`  
  _Meng Bi, Yili Jin, Kaiyuan Hu, Xize Duan, Jiaxin Huang, Hong Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[BReD: BEV Residual Diffusion for Feed-Forward Road Gaussian Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28191)**  `arXiv:2611.28191`  
  _Baizhi Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate road surface reconstruction is essential for autonomous-driving mapping and simulation, but existing methods trade reconstruction quality for cross-scene inference. Optimization-based methods recover detailed surfaces through costly per-scene optimization, while feed-forward methods lack road-specific constraints and often produce large elevation errors. We propose \textbf{BReD}, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing road elevation, appearance, and semantics from calibrated six-camera sequences. BReD first estimates coarse elevation through LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only cameras at inference. A lightweight BEV residual diffusion model then conditions elevation refinement on a camera-derived depth--elevation discrepancy and elevation-aware image features. Diffusion-indexed perturbations expose the model to different discrepancy corruption levels during training, while inference performs one deterministic refinement from the clean discrepancy. The refined elevations are temporally aggregated to anchor road-aligned Gaussians, whose attributes are predicted by a geometry-prior-guided decoder without test-time optimization. On four held-out nuScenes scenes, BReD achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92\% semantic mIoU, compared with 14.43 cm for RoGS without test-time LiDAR and 8.88 cm for its test-time-LiDAR-assisted variant; both RoGS variants require per-scene optimization.
  </details>

- **[Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28177)**  `arXiv:2611.28177`  
  _Willi Poh, Kevin Rösch, Christoph Stiller_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.
  </details>

- **[Med-Agentic: Distilling Agentic Medical Reasoning with Internalized Meta-Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28176)**  `arXiv:2611.28176`  
  _Yucheng Zhou, Junwei Sheng, Jianbing Shen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) in expert domains face a trade-off between agentic tool use, which externalizes expertise behind brittle multi-turn runtimes, and end-to-end specialization, which internalizes expertise only implicitly at task-level granularity. We propose internalized meta-capabilities: atomic, parametrically internalized, and composable reasoning units that an LLM can select and combine within a single chain-of-thought (CoT). We instantiate this idea as Med-Agentic for medical visual diagnosis, where the model emits a capability-tagged structured CoT in one forward pass, turning capability invocation into tagged token generation rather than external tool calls. For training, Med-OPD performs multi-teacher on-policy distillation with token-level dual-factor teacher routing conditioned on both the image and the active capability tag, strictly generalizing per-prompt teacher routing. We show that this routing gives an unbiased estimator of the same expected teacher-KL gradient. Across public medical imaging datasets spanning nine anatomies and eight modalities, Med-Agentic consistently improves in-distribution and out-of-distribution diagnostic accuracy over the strong competitors.
  </details>

- **[VideoJSON: A Minimal Harness Beats Purpose-Built Memory for Ultra-Long Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28167)**  `arXiv:2611.28167`  
  _Wenqi Marshall Guo, Kuan-Hao Huang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points.   </details>

- **[Dynamics-Guided Conditional MeanFlow from Regional Interaction to Internal Revision and Its Application to CT Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28139)**  `arXiv:2611.28139`  
  _Md Shifatul Ahsan Apurba, Md Selim, Jin Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Although one-step flow models reduce inference costs and iterative restoration methods introduce subsequent corrections, how predicted transformation dynamics can guide internal feature refinement remains underexplored. We introduce IRCMF, a dynamics-guided Conditional MeanFlow framework that combines regional interaction with recurrent internal revision. The decoder predicts signed interval velocity and a learned velocity-change cue. A soft-region graph aggregates contextual information for velocity estimation, while a dynamics-conditioned graph establishes regional relationships to guide recurrent bottleneck updates. The revised features are processed by the shared decoder to recompute velocity, establishing feedback between transformation dynamics and internal representations. An actor-critic policy controls regional updates and further revisions to balance enhancement quality and computational cost. We evaluate IRCMF on two computed tomography (CT) datasets, NLST for STANDARD-to-LUNG kernel enhancement and LDCT-and-Projection-data for simulated low-to-routine-dose enhancement. With nine decoder evaluations, IRCMF achieves slice-level PSNR of $36.24 \pm 3.49$ dB and SSIM of $0.97 \pm 0.01$ on NLST, and PSNR of $32.45 \pm 1.97$ dB and SSIM of $0.84 \pm 0.05$ on LDCT-and-Projection-data. The learned policy reduces average decoder evaluations to 4.42 and 3.45, respectively, lowering per-slice latency from 97.00 to 51.82 ms and from 97.12 to 41.95 ms, with PSNR reductions of only 0.20 and 0.06 dB.
  </details>

- **[Choose What Returns: Object-Aware KV Memory for Selective Recall in Interactive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28137)**  `arXiv:2611.28137`  
  _Hyunwook Kang, Junoh Park, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
  </details>

- **[ENGRAM: Reliability-Weighted Latent Fusion and Occlusion-Aware Layered Readout for Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28136)**  `arXiv:2611.28136`  
  _Chenhao Wu, Zhaolong Su, Yang Liu, Tianrui Su, Yingguang Yang, Shang Luo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Camera-conditioned video world models aim to generate 3D-consistent videos from a single image along specified camera trajectories. However, set-union updates in latent spatial memory leave repeated observations unconsolidated, while frontmost-only readout limits simultaneous access to stored evidence at different depths. To address these limitations, we present ENGRAM, a latent spatial memory framework combining reliability-weighted latent fusion and occlusion-aware layered readout. Specifically, recursive fusion integrates geometrically and visually compatible observations in a channel-normalized latent space, consolidating repeated evidence into a shared scene representation. Layered readout exposes multiple depth-ordered latent candidates with their reliability and availability at each target cell. This gives the generator access to information from multiple surfaces as visibility changes. Explicit camera rays provide viewpoint information independently of memory coverage, while geometric consistency constraints guide memory updates. Memory retrieval uses a single projection at latent resolution, avoiding intermediate RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding. We adapt a pretrained video generator using only 256 training scenes. On 100 RealEstate10K test scenes, ENGRAM improves novel-view-synthesis and closed-loop PSNRs over Spatia by 0.82 and 4.48 dB, respectively. On a 200-case WorldScore evaluation subset, it achieves an average score of 67.78, exceeding Spatia by 3.31 points. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Output Suppression: Mitigating Privacy Risks in LVLMs via Visual Intrinsic Privacy Erasure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28135)**  `arXiv:2611.28135`  
  _Xiangkui Cao, Jie Zhang, Meina Kan, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large vision-language models can extract personally identifiable information from images, making privacy protection essential for their deployment in perception-oriented tasks. Existing targeted fine-tuning and model-editing methods usually suppress sensitive answers by aligning the model toward safe responses. In this paper, we show that such protection can be illusory: although the fine-tuned model refuses to disclose private information under normal decoding, privacy leakage still occurs in sentence completion scenarios. This indicates that existing algorithms only change the model's output distribution, but the model still retains the ability to perceive private information. Private information therefore still remains inside the model. To address this problem, we propose Visual Intrinsic Privacy Erasure (VIPE), which targets privacy-related visual representations to weaken the model's ability to perceive sensitive information. VIPE constructs paired privacy-sensitive and privacy-masked images, uses their internal feature residuals to identify privacy-related visual components, and suppresses these components before they are perceived by the model. To preserve benign visual representations, the erasure objective projects feature differences onto a relaxed benign subspace and adaptively controls the erasure strength. VIPE compels the model to ignore the extraction of sensitive information in the visual representation space, thereby blocking the source of privacy leakage more fundamentally rather than merely altering the model's output distribution. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-OneVision show that VIPE substantially alleviates prefix-triggered privacy leakage while maintaining competitive utility on general visual-language benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[SceneTether: Activity-Gated Value Anchoring for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Image Animation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28134)**  `arXiv:2611.28134`  
  _Matiur Rahman Minar, Seunghun Oh, Ganghyeon Jeong, Unsang Park_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Urban State Representation for Autonomous Mobility: A Survey of Multimodal Perception, Architectures, Datasets, and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28129)**  `arXiv:2611.28129`  
  _Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[DINO-KNN: Training-Free Multiclass In-Context Segmentation via Nearest Neighbors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28127)**  `arXiv:2611.28127`  
  _Hussain Alasmawi, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In-context segmentation (ICS) segments a target image given a few annotated reference images. Recent training-free methods built on frozen foundation models segment one class at a time and gain little from additional references. We study the multiclass, multi-reference setting and ask how far a simple joint decision rule can go. We introduce DINO-KNN, which stores every labeled reference patch of a frozen DINOv3 encoder in a single memory and labels each target patch by a distance-weighted vote of its k nearest neighbors. All classes are predicted in a single pass, with one label per pixel, without training or a mask decoder. We evaluate on eight datasets, four natural and four medical, with R=1 to 15 reference images and three reference seeds. DINO-KNN achieves the best average mIoU at every R; it is the best method on six of the eight datasets from R=3 and on seven of the eight from R=7. Its accuracy continues to grow with the number of references, from 37.8 mIoU at R=1 to 56.2 at R=15, while the strongest baseline, INSID3, rises from 36.1 to 42.9. DINO-KNN is also 2.1x faster than INSID3. The code will be made public.
  </details>

- **[ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28124)**  `arXiv:2611.28124`  
  _Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
  </details>

- **[Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28123)**  `arXiv:2611.28123`  
  _Yiyang Zhu, Xin Li, Guangyuan Liu, Ziheng Liu, Jiayi Zhang, Chau Yuen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
  </details>

- **[RALC: Risk-Controlled Local Adoption of Segmentation Updates with Few Calibration Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28122)**  `arXiv:2611.28122`  
  _Shize Yin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fine-tuning a road-scene segmenter for rain and nighttime driving can introduce errors on normal daytime images. With few labeled normal images for calibration, a whole-image risk check may reject changes that would pass if adopted locally. Risk-Controlled Adoption of Label Changes (RALC) selects local changes from a fixed model update, using confidence differences and an image score to form nested candidates. On each normal calibration image, RALC measures how many more errors each candidate makes than the original model, assigning zero loss when errors stay the same or fall. At test time, each replacement can add at most one error, so the replacement count bounds the net increase without test labels. RALC combines this candidate-dependent bound with recorded calibration losses to select the largest set that passes the risk check. If the models and adoption rules are fixed before calibration and normal calibration and test images are exchangeable, the expected per-image loss stays within budget. On held-out BDD100K, we evaluated three weight-interpolated updates with 10 additional normal images per calibration draw. At a common fixed budget, adverse-scene mIoU was 1.89--3.19 percentage points higher with RALC than with whole-image adoption, while measured mean normal loss was also higher. After matching this loss post hoc at 1,000 pixels per image, RALC still led by 1.135--2.428 points. Selecting changes in $8\times8$-pixel cells recovered 93--98% of this advantage. With 250 calibration images at the original budget, both rules adopted all three updates in full.
  </details>

- **[Seeing Beyond Pixels: Radar Feature Generation from Images and Sparse Returns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28119)**  `arXiv:2611.28119`  
  _Hongyu Zhou, Yubo Peng, Luping Xiang, Kun Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Camera-radar fusion benefits from complementary visual and geometric information but often relies on complete radar representations, leading to substantial computing overhead. However, the extent to which visual information can compensate for limited radar measurements remains insufficiently explored. Therefore, we propose Vision-informed Radar Token Generation (VRTG), which exploits cross-modal information to generate task-relevant radar features from camera images and sparse radar measurements. Specifically, VRTG first leverages image-derived object cues to select a limited number of informative radar points. It then establishes calibrated one-to-one associations between visual objects and radar returns, using matched measurements to refine object ranges while retaining visual estimates for unmatched objects. Finally, the associated object features and visual context are transformed into radar tokens compatible with existing camera-radar fusion networks. Experiments on RADIal demonstrate that VRTG achieves 90.76\% vehicle-detection F1 and 86.68\% free-space mIoU using only four radar points per frame, approaching the performance of the full-radar model.
  </details>

- **[StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28118)**  `arXiv:2611.28118`  
  _Qing Mu, Jiani Zheng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity.We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.
  </details>

- **[PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28117)**  `arXiv:2611.28117`  
  _Zihan Deng, Xinpei Lin, Du Tiantian, Lequan Yu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.
  </details>

- **[Is It the Agent or the Retry? Separating Selection from Agency in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28116)**  `arXiv:2611.28116`  
  _Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic text-to-image systems wrap generators in loops of planning, routing, verification and refinement, and report large gains on compositional benchmarks, almost always relative to a single sample. We ask how much of the gain survives against Single-tool Rejection Retry (\ours): the strongest generator already in the system's pool, an off-the-shelf verifier, and retries that stop at the first accepted image under the system's own budget. Auditing four recent systems with official evaluators, we find that on GenEval SRR matches the accuracy of OctoT2I (0.962 vs.\ 0.96), recovers 63 to 90% of the gain of GEMS depending on the verifier, and exceeds GenPilot by 12 points with 2.3 generations per image; the effect persists with generators not tuned to the benchmark and on T2I-CompBench++. A closed-form analysis predicts the accuracy of SRR at every budget and shows that its gain is capped by the verifier's likelihood ratio. The same analysis also exposes genuine agentic gains: on GenEval 2, even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator stays 15 points below the score GEMS reports (12 at the upper end of its 95% interval). We prove a ceiling on the accuracy that routing across generators can add, bracket it between one and three points on OctoT2I's own pool, and show that what OctoT2I's routing buys is compute (about 2.5less than SRR at equal accuracy), not accuracy. In our offline distillation experiments selected samples teach the generator no more than random ones, which a short information argument explains. We end with a reporting checklist for agentic generation papers.
  </details>

- **[NOVA: Normalization-Aware Output-Guided Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28115)**  `arXiv:2611.28115`  
  _Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator.We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
  </details>

- **[Benchmarking Foundation Models for Bone Scaffold Pore Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Few-Shot Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28113)**  `arXiv:2611.28113`  
  _Tri Tin Vo, Vu Thien An Ngo, Nhi Kieu, Cuong Hung Luu, Giang V. H. Phan, Kien Nguyen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating the mechanical properties of bone scaffolds conventionally requires destructive testing or costly Finite Element Analysis, while deep learning alternatives are constrained by the scarcity of labeled biomaterial imaging data. This study introduces the first expert-annotated, pixel-dense dataset of biopolymer bone-scaffold SEM images, spanning five magnification series, and uses it to benchmark two state-of-the-art pre-trained foundation models under a 12-shot fine-tuning regime. SAM3, an instance segmenter, and YOLOv26, a bounding-box detector, feed the predicted pore geometry to regression heads that estimate Young's modulus and compressive yield strength. Our central finding is that both models fail by pore density rather than magnification: YOLOv26's predicted pore counts saturate and porosity estimation collapses on the most crowded frames, whereas SAM3 over-fragments sparse pore fields and merges adjacent pores in dense ones, producing eight catastrophic failures against three for YOLOv26. Averaged across the 44-image evaluation set, YOLOv26 achieves lower porosity error (19.9% vs. 23.1% MAE), higher precision, and a higher F1 score, whereas SAM3 offers pixel-level instance segmentation that YOLOv26's bounding boxes cannot reproduce. We conclude that model selection should be driven by pore density rather than SEM magnification alone.
  </details>

- **[ROSE-SAM3: Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28112)**  `arXiv:2611.28112`  
  _Yanghui Song, Chengfu Yang, Yongpeng Wen, Zhanxuan Hu, Wei Lu, Qi Ming, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[GC-GS: Optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting with Gradient Conflict as a Geometry Signal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28111)**  `arXiv:2611.28111`  
  _Chenhao Zhang, Fengze Zhang, Fengqing Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.
  </details>
