- **[Tangent incompleteness under coupled image transformations: margin reconstruction and decision consequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28110)**  `arXiv:2611.28110`  
  _Karim Bounja, Abdeljalil Sakat_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can accurate responses to individual geometric image transformations recover their combined effect on a classifier's decision? For identity-aligned bilinear resampling, coordinatewise assembly may fail at first order. Projecting the implemented transformation onto a fixed logit-margin gradient, we derive a linear term plus signed absolute-value ridges. An exact even--odd identity and ridge-cancellation conditions characterize the missing information. Under independent parameter laws, a noncancelling off-coordinate ridge obstructs even unrestricted additive fits. The coupled correction has $O(s^2)$ projected error, versus a possible $\Theta(s)$ axiswise defect; transfer to realized network margins requires local smoothness. Projected RMS errors fall by 82.96% on CIFAR-10 and 82.38% on ImageNetV2 relative to axiswise assembly; realized fixed-pair margin RMS errors fall by 39.75% and 42.73%. The representation prospectively identifies nine strict nonadditive network-margin sign configurations and permits exact minimization of a three-parameter threat surrogate, with conditional selection-regret guarantees. In an independent CIFAR-10 search, coupled-selected transformations uncover 51 top-1 changes versus 41 for axes. On 256 independent ImageNetV2/ConvNeXt-Tiny images and 16,384 transformed decisions at the prespecified scale $s=.40$, multiclass top-1 flip-prediction errors fall from 11.97% to 10.23% (paired improvement 1.74 percentage points; 95% interval [0.93, 2.61]). Directional finite differences are slightly more accurate (10.00%) at higher measured model-construction cost. These results connect first-order sampling interactions to margin reconstruction, decision prediction, and threat selection, without claiming finite-scale network certification.
  </details>

- **[Cyclic Discrete Diffusion: A Novel Multi-Class Segmentation Refinement Technique](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28107)**  `arXiv:2611.28107`  
  _Libo Chen, Souvik Ghosh, Vinay P. Namboodiri_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We cast image segmentation refinement as a discrete diffusion process. To solve this task we introduce Cyclic Discrete Diffusion (CDD), a novel forward-reverse formulation with a cyclic label topology that maps a discrete label set to the uniform distribution and back. Instead of injecting Gaussian noise as is done for continuous diffusion, CDD evolves segmentation masks through label jumps: at each step, every pixel either remains in its current class or jumps to the next label with a fixed rate. This jump-or-stay mechanism defines a finite-state Markov process with bounded forward and reverse steps, featuring analytically consistent and tractable reverse dynamics. CDD operates natively in a multi-class label space, enabling joint refinement of all classes in a single pass without requiring class-wise decomposition, as commonly needed in prior binary refinement approaches. The proposed formulation admits a finite and controllable number of refinement steps, for which we analyze the convergence properties through spectral gap analysis. We evaluate CDD across diverse segmentation tasks, including multi-class semantic, instance-level, and binary segmentation refinement. Our method consistently improves both region accuracy and boundary quality across multiple backbones and datasets.
  </details>

- **[Gradient-Free Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision Models via Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28105)**  `arXiv:2611.28105`  
  _Khayrul Islam_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Adapting a vision model to new classes from a few labeled images usually relies on gradient fine-tuning, which is unstable with so few images. We ask whether a coding agent can replace gradient descent for this task. We propose the Agent edit, a method in which a coding agent writes a program that sets the new class weights in the class head of a frozen COCO-trained detector, with no gradient step. The agent runs the detector on the labeled images a limited number of times and sees how much its edit lowers COCO mAP; the program rebuilds the weights without the agent. In the same head and with the same labels, the Agent edit outperforms full-decoder fine-tuning at five shots on 2 of four fine-grained sets, by 11.2 and 12.3 F1 points, and ties on the rest. At ten shots, fine-tuning ties with or outperforms it. Moreover, when the new classes are scored jointly with the COCO classes, the AP of the COCO class to which they belong falls by up to 33.3 points, and limiting that loss lowers F1 on the new classes. Most of the agent's programs share three parts, which we write as a formula that needs no agent. A classifier on frozen backbone features reaches a higher F1 than every method inside the head on every set. Hence a coding agent can replace gradient descent only in part: inside the head and at five shots.
  </details>

- **[Intervene or Trust CLIP? Competence-Gated Adaptation for Source-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28104)**  `arXiv:2611.28104`  
  _Haoyue Liu, Chenhao Zhu, Yu Huo, Haoran Shou, Shuguang Cui, Xiaoying Tang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Source-free cross-domain few-shot learning (SF-CDFSL) adapts a pre-trained vision-language model such as CLIP to a distant target domain from a handful of labeled images, without access to source data. Recent methods improve the fine-tuning of CLIP with token-level interventions and apply them in the same way to every target domain. In this paper, we find that whether an intervention helps depends on how well frozen CLIP already recognizes the target domain: in 5-way 1-shot tasks, intervening improves accuracy by 0.72 points where frozen CLIP misclassifies most support images, but lowers it by 1.31 points where frozen CLIP already classifies them well, and the support set of a single episode suffices to tell the two cases apart; a bias-variance analysis explains both. Based on this finding, we propose Competence-Gated Adaptation (CoGA), which measures frozen CLIP's accuracy and margin on the labeled support set and decides, before training, whether to intervene on the visual tokens or to trust CLIP by fusing the adapted prediction with the frozen one. CoGA adds no trainable parameters and uses no query labels. On the four BSCD-FSL target domains, CoGA achieves the best average accuracy, 59.56% (1-shot) and 68.96% (5-shot), outperforms ATHA and TIR by at least 2.82 and 1.39 points on the same episodes, and consistently improves three further backbones, three parameter-efficient fine-tuning frameworks and five further target domains.
  </details>

- **[Scale-Aware Reference Attention for Mannequin-to-Model Gown Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28101)**  `arXiv:2611.28101`  
  _Guang Yang, Fengchen Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Formal gowns are sold online with photos of models wearing them, and buyers zoom in to inspect sequins, lace and beading. Image editors can turn a photo of a gown on a mannequin into a convincing photo of a person wearing it, but they receive every reference photo without any notion of its magnification, and the fine detail of the gown is lost when the output is viewed up close. We propose scale-aware reference attention (SARA), which tells an open diffusion transformer the zoom level of the output and of every reference photo, biases the attention of the output toward references of a similar zoom level, uses macro photos of the fabric as references, and is trained on a mix of whole-garment and zoomed targets. To train and evaluate it, we introduce Kiss3000, a dataset of 915 high-resolution mannequin photos and 2274 on-model photos of formal gowns with cross-domain pairs and splits by style, and zoom-crop evaluation, which compares garment crops at full, half and local scale without pixel alignment and judges local fidelity with two vision-language models gated on control crops. With this protocol, Nano Banana Pro at 4K, the highest-resolution commercial editor we test, loses or redraws local detail on 14 of 20 test gowns. At 1536x2048 pixels, both judges prefer SARA over a LoRA fine-tuning baseline on 18 test items and the baseline on 6 (p=0.023), and over the base model on 26 against 4 (p=5.9e-5), while SARA keeps the gown design as often as the baseline.
  </details>

- **[You Only Think Once: Rescuing Hybrid Vision-Language Models Lost in Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28100)**  `arXiv:2611.28100`  
  _Tianyi Tan, Wentao Wang, Xiaohan Li, Zining Ren, Siyuan Li, Xutao Mao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.
  </details>

- **[VidRouteBench: A Benchmark for Budgeted Video-Generation Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28099)**  `arXiv:2611.28099`  
  _Dayu Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each.We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none.We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.
  </details>

- **[ORDO: Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Video LLMs via Order-Dependent Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28097)**  `arXiv:2611.28097`  
  _Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
  </details>

- **[When Recognition Meets Discovery: Learning Need Not Be Entangled in One Representation Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28092)**  `arXiv:2611.28092`  
  _Chenglin Liu, An Tian, Mingxuan Du, Shang Rui Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled data containing both old and novel samples. Existing methods typically optimize recognition and discovery within a shared representation space, implicitly assuming that the same representation geometry can serve both objectives. Through controlled spectral analysis, we uncover a striking asymmetry: old-class discrimination is increasingly concentrated in the dominant singular directions, while novel-class structure is better preserved in the complementary residual space. More importantly, strengthening the former can even degrade the latter, revealing that recognition and discovery compete for representation capacity rather than merely for optimization weight. Motivated by this observation, we propose Dual-Space Spectral Routing, which dynamically decomposes the representation via online SVD and routes supervised recognition and unsupervised discovery to complementary discriminative and general subspaces. We further exploit their distinct responses to old and novel samples to construct a dual-space novelty signal, which guides Subspace Relation Aggregation (SRA) for organizing candidate novel categories. Extensive experiments across multiple GCD baselines, backbones, and benchmarks demonstrate a consistently improved recognition-discovery balance without introducing additional inference parameters. Code will be open source.
  </details>

- **[Efficient Memory-Constrained Video Object Segmentation via Subspace Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28087)**  `arXiv:2611.28087`  
  _Hai-Anh Le, Le-Trung Nguyen, Enzo Tartaglione_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Memory-based architectures for video object segmentation (VOS) have achieved remarkable performance by maintaining dense feature representations from past frames in a streaming Memory Bank. However, storing these features over time incurs substantial memory overhead and computational cost. In this work, we identify significant temporal redundancy in memory representations, where consecutive frames exhibit highly overlapping low-rank subspaces that remain stable over time. Building on this observation, we propose Memory Subspace Iteration (MSI), a training-free, model-agnostic plugin that exploits temporal subspace stability to efficiently compress streaming memory features. Extensive experiments on standard VOS benchmarks demonstrate that MSI preserves segmentation accuracy across multiple architectures while reducing the memory bank footprint by up to 25%. Our implementation is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[UbiEnlight: User-Perception-Aware Real-Time Low-Light Video Enhancement on Mobile Devices and Smartglasses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28085)**  `arXiv:2611.28085`  
  _Minfan Wang, Sicong Liu, Teng Li, Zimu Zhou, Sixun He, Bin Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Low-light video capture is now common on smartphones and wearables, yet dynamic illumination coupled with mobile/werable user motion causes noise, blur, and flicker that make videos hard to perceive and use, especially for users with night blindness and near-eye displays. Prior work enhances frames with post-hoc temporal constraints or optimizes videos directly; however,low-light and motion degradations are spatiotemporally coupled, so post-hoc consistency after per-frame restoration often leaves flicker and motion artifacts. We present UbiEnlight, the first diffusion-transformer-based on-device system for real-time, temporally stable low-light video enhancement. UbiEnlight builds on two insights: (1) illumination and structure separate more robustly in the frequency domain, enabling a spectrum-guided diffusion transformer that injects Fourier amplitude/phase priors to correct illumination while anchoring structure without optical flow; and (2) user perceptual tolerance varies by context, motivating a perception-aware controller that adapts sampling depth, attention reuse, and frame caching at runtime. We implement UbiEnlight on smartphones and smartglasses, and evaluate it against state-of-the-art baselines. UbiEnlight improves temporal stability by up to 54.76% under dynamic/extreme conditions while sustaining real-time on-device performance.
  </details>

- **[ReSUL: Learning Regional Sensor Utility for Robust Multisensor Semantic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28084)**  `arXiv:2611.28084`  
  _Yiwen Wang, Jiahao Qin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A corrupted sensor observation is not necessarily useless: misalignment can place informative scene structure at the wrong location. Robust multisensor segmentation must determine where to retain this evidence, where to exclude it, and where repair can recover its value. We introduce Regional Sensor Utility Learning (ReSUL), which learns these choices through their effect on segmentation risk. ReSUL compares full-sensor predictions, sensor-exclusion paths, and a re-registration path for displaced thermal inputs. A router predicts each path's signed reduction in category-balanced Brier risk relative to a fixed reference, then uses these estimates to allocate spatial mixture weights. This supervision connects spatial allocation to measurable task benefit without requiring fault labels at inference. MFNet experiments compare project-trained models under eleven clean and disturbed input conditions. ReSUL ranks first in 10 of 11 conditions in both ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-22k comparisons. Under severe thermal displacement, it reaches 54.58% and 55.63% mIoU, exceeding the strongest competing method in each group by 7.19 and 5.63 percentage points. Fixed-bank MFNet ablations show that utility supervision improves all eleven condition means over task-only routing. These results support learning how to use disturbed observations through their regional prediction benefit. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[OSLA: Observation-Aware Local Alignment and Cross-Scene Relation Learning for Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28083)**  `arXiv:2611.28083`  
  _Xinyang Zhang, Feiyu Han, Chenhao Wu, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Yingguang Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification (AS-ReID) aims to retrieve identities across spectral modalities and aerial-ground viewpoints using a unified model. However, changes in viewpoint and spectrum can make local correspondences unreliable, while conventional sampling may omit cross-camera positive relations needed for training. To address these challenges, we propose OSLA, an observation-aware framework built on supervised CLIP-ReID that combines Local Identity Alignment (LIA) and Cross-Scene Relation Learning (CSR). Specifically, LIA uses historical identity observations and competing-identity information to select reliable cross-scene local correspondences while allowing unmatched regions. Local-to-global distillation transfers identity knowledge from correctly classified historical local features into the global representation. CSR couples observed-cell sampling with spectrum-grouped ranking to jointly organize and optimize cross-camera relations. Sampling across two cameras and two spectra provides same- and cross-spectrum positives, while ranking constrains positive-negative scores separately by gallery spectrum on the final retrieval descriptor. Both modules operate only during training, preserving the original visual encoder and retrieval descriptor at inference. Experiments on WHU-MARS-1000 and WHU-MARS-2337 demonstrate that OSLA achieves absolute Rank-1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8% over UAD, respectively, under the AS-ReID protocol. The code will be available.
  </details>

- **[BehaviorICL: Task-Conditioned Decoder States for Visual In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28081)**  `arXiv:2611.28081`  
  _Chenyang Wang, Jiamo Hu, Chengrui Wu, Lingyue Chen, Jianguo Chen, Xun Xu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.
  </details>

- **[Multimodal Violence Understanding and Temporal Retrieval in Movies with Adaptive Audio-Visual Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28080)**  `arXiv:2611.28080`  
  _Jiaqian Li, Rohitash Chandra_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.
  </details>

- **[Vision-Language Truck Driving Advisories Grounded in Provincial Rules and Forecast Risks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28079)**  `arXiv:2611.28079`  
  _Xintong Jiang, Shucheng Huang, Qiaoxuan Zhang, Jincheng Xu, Yukun Lu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) can generate context-aware driving advisories, but their outputs may conflict with road conditions or traffic rules, and they typically address a hazard only once it is visible. This matters for long-haul trucking, where heavy trucks need long stopping distances and a single trip may cross several jurisdictions with different traffic regulations. This paper proposes a data generation and distillation framework that integrates structured scene understanding, risk forecasting, and traffic-rule retrieval to generate truck driving decisions and natural-language advisories, with a consistency check on every record. The records, written by an 8B teacher, are then used to distill a 3B-parameter student model for onboard deployment. We also introduce a dashcam dataset covering four Canadian provinces, comprising 11,142 annotated lane-marking frames and 9,494 driving segments. On held-out driving data across all four provinces, the student passes the consistency check in 94.6% of the segments, against 20.2% for the untuned 8B teacher, and announces 26.2% of the risks in the next 10 to 30 seconds before they appear. Of the generated advisories, 97.7% conform to the provincial traffic rules and guidance. These findings suggest that the framework can produce rule-conforming training data for compact driving advisory models.
  </details>

- **[Adversarial Attacks Expose Path-Dependent Failures in Discrete Medical Image Tokenizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28078)**  `arXiv:2611.28078`  
  _Ahmed Loughzali, Akash Yallamati, Aadiv Reki, Aslan Shaukat Vaida, Jeyashree Krishnan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Discrete image tokenizers convert medical images into token sequences that downstream models either decode into an image for a classifier (the reconstruction path), classify directly (the token path), or feed to a generative multimodal model. We ask whether imperceptible input perturbations can break these systems through the tokenizer alone. We evaluate four tokenizers on three imaging modalities and extend the strongest attack to a deployed generative model. Our central finding is path-dependence: the same tokenizer fails in opposite ways depending on how its output is used. A supervised attack collapses diagnostic accuracy on the reconstruction path, with ROC AUC falling to $\leq 0.013$ at $\epsilon=2/255$ on all four tokenizers, while sparing the token path. An unsupervised, label-free attack does the reverse; its damage concentrates in the multi-codebook tokenizers, worst in MedITok, whose token-path AUC falls from 0.919 to 0.239. The same label-free attack transfers to LLaVA-Med, a frozen medical vision-language model built on MedITok, making it report proliferative diabetic retinopathy in a healthy retina or call a malignant lesion benign, without access to the question, answer, or language-model gradients. Harm is driven by how far the attack moves the tokenizer's internal representation, not by how many tokens change: on the learned-codebook tokenizers, a control attack that changes nearly all tokens but moves the representation less leaves every path and answer intact. Domain-specific pretraining does not provide robustness: MedITok has the best clean accuracy yet is the most fragile, more so than UniTok, its general-domain counterpart. None of six candidate defenses repairs every failure mode, and several fail once the attacker optimizes against the defense directly. Medical tokenizer robustness must therefore be evaluated per downstream path, against an adaptive adversary.
  </details>

- **[Fairness Evaluation for Diffusion and Flow Models Should Account for the Generation Path: Implications for Clinical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28077)**  `arXiv:2611.28077`  
  _Dharini Raghavan, Amritpal Singh, Anant Madabhushi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Medical image generation models are often evaluated using images produced by a single sampling procedure. However, diffusion and flow models can use different numbers of sampling steps, sampling schedules, or numerical solvers without changing their trained parameters. These changes may affect the generated images and the clinical measurements derived from them. We argue that fairness results obtained under one sampling procedure should not be assumed to hold under another, particularly when changes in sampling affect clinical task errors differently across patient groups. Building on previous work on medical image quality, accelerated sampling, generation dynamics, and generative model fairness, we examine why the sampling procedure should be considered part of the evaluated system. We define subgroup differences in clinical task error across sampling procedures and provide a mathematical example showing that two groups can have identical outputs under the exact dynamics and a reference sampler but different errors under an alternative sampler. We also extend this result to stochastic generation under shared noise. An exploratory experiment with an age-conditioned image generation model illustrates how changing the number and timing of sampling steps can alter image-derived measurements, although these differences do not establish clinical unfairness. We therefore argue that fairness evaluation should assess the sampling procedure used in practice and examine intermediate generation states when they help explain differences in clinically relevant errors across patient groups. Analysis code is available herethis https URL
  </details>

- **[StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27915)**  `arXiv:2611.27915`  
  _Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
  </details>

- **[Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27780)**  `arXiv:2611.27780`  
  _Chengchao Lv, Yin Wang, Chunzheng Zhu, Wanli Chang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.
  </details>

- **[Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27585)**  `arXiv:2611.27585`  
  _Ignazio Gallo, Mattia Gatti, Leonardo Sgroi, Darwin Castillo, Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona, Nicola Landro_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above every imaging arm we evaluated (best 0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, reproduces every finding except legibility, from a confounder that is clinically legitimate. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.
  </details>

- **[PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27521)**  `arXiv:2611.27521`  
  _Silviu-Florin Gheorghe, Radu-Stefan Popa, Adriana Valentina Costache, Adrian-Gabriel Chifu, Alessia Amelio, Paul Irofti, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Beyond What They Say: Cue Acknowledgment and Robustness in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27389)**  `arXiv:2611.27389`  
  _Ali Rahimiakbar, Arvin Baghal Asl, Nima Niroumand, Mohammad Parsa Jafarnejady, Hossein Shahabadi, Amirmohammad Izadi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Explanations are used to assess whether vision-language models rely on visual evidence or misleading suggestions. A response that explicitly names a cue can still follow it, making disclosure alone an incomplete basis for judging robustness. We ask whether greater cue acknowledgment accompanies greater resistance. We compare matched answers and explanations under helpful, misleading, and conflicting visual and textual cues while holding the underlying question and correct answer fixed. A paired comparison shows that a model can select the endorsed wrong answer more often while acknowledging the cues more often. Reduced silence therefore need not indicate improved resistance. Explanations may also mention a textual suggestion while omitting an accompanying visual cue. Requesting evidence and acknowledgment does not consistently improve resistance in the tested settings. Outcomes vary across models and settings, and these comparisons do not isolate a causal effect of acknowledgment. Evaluations should report cue following and acknowledgment on the same instances, distinguishing visual from textual cues.
  </details>

- **[Zing-1.0: A Playable World System Built on Controllable Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27336)**  `arXiv:2611.27336`  
  _Wenbo Zhang, Guoli Zhang, Xuewen Yu, Xueliang Yang, Jiangqiao Yan, Teng Xia, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. An executable engine resolves player actions under the world's rules and produces proxy video from the updated state. A streaming video model synthesizes the player's view from this proxy, and the runtime delivers it to inform subsequent actions. (1) Principle and system. We formulate Controllable Rendering and define the interfaces among world construction, world execution, observation synthesis, and the interaction runtime. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation-independent specification of a Playable World System. (2) AI-native engine. WorldKit provides structured authoring tools and reusable character, camera, and control components for coding agents to construct executable proxy worlds. It supports extensible interactions and precise geometric motion control while separating executable behavior from final visual appearance. (3) Streaming renderer. We adapt MiniMax-H3 for block-causal autoregressive generation and incremental decoding. Proxy video constrains structure and motion, while text and separate scene and subject references specify appearance. We train the generator on diverse tasks and distill it to generate each block in a few denoising steps. The renderer leads the compared streaming editors on OpenVE (3.90) and LongV2VBench (3.44). On StreamEval, Zing-1.0 scores 57.86 on instruction editing and 54.06 on reference editing, exceeding the published baselines on both tracks. (4) Interaction infrastructure. We build an Interaction Runtime that routes player actions to WorldKit while supporting in-play prompt and reference updates. Cross-block joint execution and sparse attention with compressed K/V reduce inference overhead. With the DiT on a single H200 and encoding and decoding on one H100 each, the serving system achieves a steady-state throughput of 23.82 FPS at $832\times480$.
  </details>

- **[Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27166)**  `arXiv:2611.27166`  
  _Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26380)**  `arXiv:2611.26380`  
  _Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu, Rundong Wang, Zongyang Qiu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
  </details>

- **[C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26316)**  `arXiv:2611.26316`  
  _Esha Sadia Nasir, Jiaqi Lv, Gozde N. Gunesli, Shan E Ahmed Raza_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.
  </details>

- **[FlexVSR: Continuous-Scale Super-Resolution for Streaming Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26178)**  `arXiv:2611.26178`  
  _Ji Wang, Haonan An, Jiasheng Zhang, Renlong Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Real-time streaming video generation has gained rapid momentum in live content creation and interactive media. Deploying such systems in practice requires flexible scaling factors to accommodate diverse source resolutions, target displays, and computational budgets. However, extending fixed-scale generative video super-resolution (VSR) to varying target scales poses two challenges: downsampling from a larger fixed scale incurs redundant cost, while re-optimizing the diffusion transformer (DiT) is costly and alters the shared generative prior. To address both, we propose FlexVSR, a decoupled framework for continuous-scale streaming generative VSR with supervision at only a few scales. Our key insight is that naively resampling fixed-scale latents onto a new target grid induces scale-dependent input mismatch, which can be effectively addressed through parameter-efficient, scale-aware adaptation of the latent interface without updating the DiT. To this end, FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a lightweight latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before they enter the DiT, enabling a shared frozen VSR prior to generalize across continuous scales with only 0.274M trainable parameters and an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, while introducing no additional temporal dependencies and preserving the native causal streaming protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming baselines and offline methods, and effective generalization to unseen continuous scales, filling the continuous-scale gap in real-time streaming generative VSR.
  </details>

- **[LIFT: Lifting Language-Controlled Image Fusion to Free-Viewpoint 3D Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25696)**  `arXiv:2611.25696`  
  _Jingning Tian, Hao Zhang, Yumin Huang, Zizhuo Li, Xingyu Jiang, Erdun Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.
  </details>

- **[LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25595)**  `arXiv:2611.25595`  
  _Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
  </details>

- **[Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25513)**  `arXiv:2611.25513`  
  _Junghoon Seo, Hakjin Lee, Jaehoon Sim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSE-Pose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[Real Cameras are Radiometric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25265)**  `arXiv:2611.25265`  
  _Ties Harder, Felix Seegräber, David Nakath, Hendrik Sauer, Kevin Köser, James Pritts_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose the radiometric camera, a model that lifts any central geometric camera model to a radiometric one. The lifted model keeps the projection of the geometric model and adds a finite aperture, a free-form focus surface and a generic vignetting function. We calibrate it by inverse rendering directly on the relative irradiance of the sensor, from the same images of standard calibration targets used in geometric calibration. Geometric calibration absorbs the bias of its feature detections. The proposed radiometric calibration uses no features, and our radiometric cameras have lower reprojection errors on held-out test sets. The focus surface extends defocus modeling from the thin lens to any central camera, and we use it in a first multi-view radiometric reconstruction, which recovers the in-focus reflectance of a texture from defocused images. The vignetting is estimated jointly and accurately reproduces a flat field measured through a diffuser. Because every standard camera model lifts to a radiometric one, the radiometric camera naturally and directly extends generative scene models beyond multi-view geometry to multi-view radiometric ones, where phenomena such as lighting and attenuation can be accurately estimated.
  </details>

- **[Self-supervised behavior encoders rarely beat a training-free baseline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24792)**  `arXiv:2611.24792`  
  _Ziwen Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Self-supervised encoders of animal and human pose are compared with one another, and rarely with simple summaries of the poses they encode. We propose such a summary that needs no training and no knowledge of the species: each body's keypoints and velocities in its own frame, a small block on the nearest other animals, and the mean, spread and histogram of every number over windows from half a second to the whole clip, reduced by PCA. We compare it with seven encoders on five benchmarks under the standard protocol: frozen representations of equal size, read by a linear classifier. It matches or beats hBehaveMAE and BAMS, the encoders pretrained on each benchmark, on all five: behaviors of mouse pairs and of human motion capture, the movements of a simulated basketball player, the strain and lighting of mouse triplets and group-level traits of flies. It leads hBehaveMAE from about a tenth of the labels. A few dozen plain kinematic measurements in place of the keypoints widen the lead over hBehaveMAE to 3.4 to 5.6 points. With all labels only HiDRA, a forecaster built for pairs of mice, beats the baseline, on mouse pairs; it trails on mouse triplets and cannot run on flies or humans. Two choices carry the baseline, the body's own frame and windows of seconds, and readouts of the frozen embeddings show what the encoders miss: they keep where body parts are, but little of how they move over seconds.
  </details>

- **[HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24731)**  `arXiv:2611.24731`  
  _Zhaolu Wang, Jiacheng Xu, Lihong Wang, Shuqing Wang, Jianjie Fang, Ziyou Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
  </details>

- **[SIRAZ: Sparse Inter-Layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-Shot Visual Neural Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23991)**  `arXiv:2611.23991`  
  _Neha, Mudasir Ganaie_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Brain-computer interfaces aim to establish direct communication between neural activity and external systems, making interpretation of brain signals an important problem. In this context, neural visual decoding seeks to infer visual information from neural activity by learning a mapping between brain responses and the corresponding visual stimuli. It investigates how visual information emerges from neural signals and relates to perceptual processing while enabling the reconstruction or retrieval of visual stimuli from neural signals. Our brain primarily follows a hierarchical pathway to process visual information captured by the eye. However, neural representations learned by existing methods differ fundamentally from those produced by the biological visual system. To bridge this gap and mimic the human vision hierarchy, we introduce Sparse Inter-layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-shot (SIRAZ). SIRAZ is a framework that aligns neural visual representations by jointly modeling early visual processes via fovea- and magnocellular-pathway-inspired Difference-of-Gaussians transformations. To align the semantic information with neural information, it extracts multiple intermediate representations of the image at multiple depths and passes them through the Residual Gated Adapter Mechanism. To study the temporal dynamics of neural signals, the Direction-aware Multi-Scale Temporal Attention Encoder is introduced to align the learned neural representation with the final visual representation. The proposed framework achieves 92.5% top-1 and 99.27% top-5 accuracy in the intra-subject setting on the THINGS-EEG dataset, and 50.25% and 75% top-1 and top-5 accuracy in the THINGS-MEG dataset. The results indicate that combining biologically motivated visual representations with the structured modalities of neural dynamics improves cross-modal alignment and zero-shot image retrieval.
  </details>

- **[SIGNTOK: A Text-Aligned Continuous Pose Tokenizer for Sign Language Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23944)**  `arXiv:2611.23944`  
  _Nabeela Khan, Gaurav Rai, Bowen Wu, Sihan Tan, Benjamin Yen, Takeshi Ashizawa, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-conditioned sign language generation (SLG) depends not only on the generator but also on the space in which signing is generated. Existing approaches generate directly in pose space, in quantized code spaces, or in learned latent spaces trained for reconstruction. We find that these spaces are organized largely by signer identity rather than linguistic content: on CSL-Daily, a test clip's nearest neighbor in raw pose space is the same sentence signed by another person in only 2% of cases. To address this, we propose SIGNTOK, a continuous pose tokenizer whose latent space is shaped by three training-only heads: a kinematics head that predicts motion dynamics, a sentence-level head that aligns signing with the overall text, and a word-level head that aligns short motion windows with content words. Together, these objectives raise the same-sentence cross-signer nearest-neighbor rate to 82%. On three sign language benchmarks, the same generator trained in the SIGNTOK latent instead of pose space raises back-translation BLEU-4 in five of six benchmark-scorer settings at comparable joint accuracy, and word-level alignment gives higher back-translation scores than sentence-level alignment on every benchmark.
  </details>

- **[Mapping the Design Space of Feature Sampling for Optical Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23822)**  `arXiv:2611.23822`  
  _Liping Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The computation of correlation features is crucial for optical flow estimation. Existing methods (e.g., RAFT) perform fixed-radius lookups on a cost volume, yielding a set of correlation features for each position; alternatively, WAFT performs single-point feature indexing, yielding one correlation feature vector per position. None of them designs a suitable correlation feature sampling scheme for each position according to regional characteristics. Our insight is that not every position requires the same sampling scheme. Applying an identical sampling scheme to every position is either redundant or insufficient and ignores the specific characteristics of the corresponding region. This paper rethinks the design of feature sampling and investigates the following question: should the support of feature sampling---i.e., the extent and directions over which evidence is aggregated---be learned separately for each query position? To study this question, we propose SAGE (Sampling with Anisotropic Gaussian Expectation). This method replaces single-point sampling with a per-pixel anisotropic Gaussian expectation on a fixed candidate grid centered on the current optical flow estimate. A positive-definite precision matrix controls the scale, anisotropy, and orientation of the sampling support, with single-point sampling included as its limiting case. Consequently, the sampling support becomes an explicit and analyzable design variable and provides a principled way to analyze how directional feature aggregation affects correspondence learning. Extensive experiments show that SAGE, while adding only 1.5% multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), effectively improves zero-shot cross-dataset generalization. When trained only on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings, SAGE reduces the end-point error (EPE) by 24.2% and 16.4% on Sintel clean and final, and reduces KITTI F1-epe and F1-all by 7.2% and 11.6%.
  </details>

- **[Practice in Text, Act in Pixels: Correcting Where Perception Fails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22722)**  `arXiv:2611.22722`  
  _Zhongling Xu, Hairong Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  GUI agents can learn cheaply from a text view of an interface and act on screenshots through a vision-language screen reader. Yet on a simulated mobile platform with a low-cost reader, policies that complete most tasks in text fail on many of the same tasks on screenshots. We ask where a small budget of real screenshots is best spent to close this gap. We find that the reader's misreads are systematic and recur on the same interface elements. Noise matched to the reader's error rates, a natural sim-to-real remedy, misses this structure, and in a pre-specified comparison it did not beat training the policy directly on screenshots. We therefore correct the misreads at their source with reader alignment, which fine-tunes the reader on screenshots paired with their text views. The reader learns to output each screen's text view, as in text practice, and the policy stays unchanged. Spent on the reader, the screenshot budget gives 80.9% full-task success on new task instances, against 55.6% when spent on training the policy. Given the same labeled screenshots, adapting the reader also beats adapting the policy, and a single aligned reader improves every text-trained policy we tried without retraining any of them.
  </details>

- **[As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22446)**  `arXiv:2611.22446`  
  _Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Jinze Liu, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Jihuai Zhu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation.In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.
  </details>

- **[PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22244)**  `arXiv:2611.22244`  
  _Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Anh Nguyen, Hong Liang, Liang Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22235)**  `arXiv:2611.22235`  
  _Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Taoyu Wu, Zhuoxiao Li, Anh Nguyen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21539)**  `arXiv:2611.21539`  
  _Zhaoning Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the match can be decoded from their hidden states. We trace where this information is lost in Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B/32B, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence, and SPair-71k semantic correspondence, comparing input-matched probes with calibrated outputs. The models fail at two distinct points. Exact copies are compared and the result reaches the answer position, but the output does not use it, whether or not the shapes have names. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but are only weakly compared and never reach the answer position. The comparison runs through 16 to 32 attention heads that let tokens of the second image attend to the first. Redistributing their attention at fixed mass removes up to 32 points of accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads, and their attention is gated by salience and weighted by content. Training only these heads (0.02% of the parameters) recovers 25 to 28 points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. Unconstrained LoRA adapters, which reach higher accuracy, converge on the same heads: inserting only these heads' attention into the base model recovers 21-51% of an adapter's gain, mostly through changed inputs to the heads. Across all 14 trained arms, the selectivity of this small head set tracks the accuracy they reach, and it is read directly from attention, without probes or retraining. The gain in selectivity is not a by-product of more attention to the first image: it comes mostly from the wrong options no longer being drawn to the marked reference.
  </details>

- **[Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Multi-Label Image Classification: A Framework, Baselines, and Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21107)**  `arXiv:2611.21107`  
  _Salih Numan Büyükbaş, Erchan Aptoula, Mamatha Thota, Petra Bosilj_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a model trained on a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain without access to the source data. Almost the entire SFDA literature assumes mutually exclusive classes, yet many deployed settings are multi-label. This paper formulates SFDA for multi-label classification and establishes the first benchmark for it: five adaptation tasks over six datasets spanning remote sensing, natural, clipart-style and driving imagery, with four single-label SFDA methods extended to provide the first baselines and a published multi-label method run alongside them, over three seeds. The benchmark shows that extending a single-label method is unreliable rather than merely suboptimal: half of the extended baselines fail to improve on the unadapted source model at all, and on two of the five tasks none of them does. The failures are not incidental. Nearest-centroid pseudo-labelling, softmax-based confidence, the diversity term of information maximization and confidence-weighted prototype construction each rely on mutual exclusivity, and each fails differently without it, so replacing the softmax with per-class sigmoids is a valid but insufficient extension. Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT) is proposed in response, a mean-teacher framework whose objective, prototype construction and alignment term are each reconsidered for overlapping label sets. It attains the best average on every reported metric and is the only method that improves on the unadapted source model on all five tasks. The analysis further introduces a prototype-agreement diagnostic separating feature-space alignment from self-reinforcing agreement with the classifier, and reports a negative result for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.
  </details>

- **[What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20000)**  `arXiv:2611.20000`  
  _Yipeng Sun, Jiajun Wang, Siyuan Mei, Yan Xia, Siming Bayer, Vincent Christlein, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.
  </details>

- **[SCALE: Towards Whole-Slide Counterfactual Explanations in Cancer Histopathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18729)**  `arXiv:2611.18729`  
  _Weiyi Qin, Yingci Liu-Swetz, Shiwei Tan, Yi Wang, Mohammad Alexanderani, Dimitrios Korentzelos, et al._
