On VIPSeg, an MLP probe trained on frozen ViT-L queries achieves conditional balanced accuracy within 0.05 percentage points of full fine-tuning, suggesting that dynamicity-relevant information is already accessible in these representations. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, the ViT-B variant achieves conditional balanced accuracies of 84.30%, 67.98%, 68.59%, and 87.64%, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance with minimal overhead in the measured inference path.
  </details>

- **[When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03429)**  `arXiv:2609.03429`  
  _Wonbin Son, Gyumun Choi, Junil Seo, Seungmin Rho, Mi Young Lee, Hyungjoon Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Answering what-if queries about a scene with a vision-language model (VLM) usually involves stating the assumption in text or editing the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is represented as a set of object tokens, and the model receives edited tokens without accompanying patch tokens from the original image. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to image-free object-token edits? We study this question in a simple testbed, keeping the visual encoder and language backbone frozen and training only a projector. Our analysis reveals three findings. Responsiveness depends on training: unlike standard VQA training, explicit edit training produces responsiveness in dense scenes and strengthens it in sparse scenes, across deletion, movement, and addition. Token construction and context token count shape responsiveness: the observed differences between token constructions appear to reflect more than token count alone, and responsiveness tends to weaken as surrounding context grows. Standard VQA performance and edit responsiveness are distinct: the object-token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-form VQA accuracy, and responses depend on the input tokens. The observed trends in responsiveness, token construction, and VQA retain their direction across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen language backbones. We release the evaluation-question generator, measurement records, scoring logs, and code.
  </details>

- **[GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28386)**  `arXiv:2608.28386`  
  _Semin Kim, Haechan Shin, Jongyoo Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing monocular full-body 3D human-object interaction (HOI) methods do not combine category-agnostic object reconstruction with finger-level contact. Their hands may float off or sink into objects, breaking realism in AR/VR environments. We present GraspHOI, the first category-agnostic framework that reconstructs a full-body 3D HOI from a single image and jointly refines the arms and fingers so that the hands meet the reconstructed object surface. GraspHOI reconstructs the body, hands, and object separately with foundation models and places them in a shared metric camera frame through depth-based registration and silhouette alignment. Occlusion-aware contact correspondences seat the object against the hand, and contact-aware optimization refines shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger rotations while anchoring the joints to the image. We find that with fingers capped near the image estimate, refining them alone is insufficient; freeing the arm removes most of the remaining hand-object gap, since in a full body the arm chain places the hand. In experiments on three datasets, GraspHOI yields more plausible hand-object contact than four baselines and better relative human-object placement than HDM and TeHOR.
  </details>

- **[Race and gender differences in medical imaging models arise at the shared decision threshold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25981)**  `arXiv:2608.25981`  
  _Mahshad Lotfinia, Daniel Truhn, Andreas Maier, Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fairness evaluations compare the performance of a medical imaging model between patient groups. A group difference in how well the model ranks images requires a better model, whereas a difference in error rates at the decision threshold shared by all groups can be addressed at the threshold. In studies of single chest radiograph models, race groups differed in error rates and hardly in ranking. However, to our knowledge, this has not been tested across image encoders, findings, and hospitals. We compared the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and false positive rate (FPR) between patient groups for 133 classification models from 13 public image encoders. The data comprised more than 700,000 images from 10 different public datasets of chest radiography, dermatology, and funduscopy. The tests resampled patients. Within each of the two hospitals with recorded race, no race difference in AUROC was statistically significant in any of the 117 chest radiograph models. By contrast, the race difference in FPR was significant in 107 models in one hospital, at a median of 12 more false positive calls per 100 radiographs without the finding, and in 54 models in the other, at a median of 6. The same held for 299 models from 22 encoders pretrained in this study with three objectives or race-balanced data and from a randomly initialized encoder. So within a hospital, the race groups differed significantly at the shared decision threshold and not in the ranking, whatever the encoder. Developers and hospitals could examine the decision threshold for each patient group before retraining a model to remove a group difference.
  </details>

- **[CoRE: Weakly Supervised Coarse-to-Fine Risk Evidence Learning in Driving Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25344)**  `arXiv:2608.25344`  
  _Kaiser Hamid, Can Cui, Nade Liang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Driver perceived risk evolves in dynamic environments and is supported by specific scene entities, yet supervision is typically limited to coarse video-level judgments. Learning when supporting evidence emerges and which entities support a risk predictor would require costly temporal- and entity-level annotations. We introduce CoRE, a weakly supervised coarse-to-fine framework that learns fine-grained prediction support from coarse video supervision. CoRE trains and freezes a video-level predictor. Structured interventions over candidate temporal regions or entity tracks measure how each candidate changes the coarse prediction, producing graded prediction-effect targets. These targets are distilled into a student that directly predicts temporal and entity support from the original video, without interventions at inference. We evaluate this learning principle across three complementary settings. RISEE tests perceived-risk support from subjective clip-level judgments without temporal or entity-level risk annotations. DoTA provides independent temporal event annotations for evaluating weakly supervised traffic-anomaly localization. UCF-Crime tests whether the same coarse-to-fine mechanism extends to a standard non-driving anomaly-detection benchmark. Across these settings, CoRE learns informative fine-grained support from coarse supervision, with strong temporal localization on DoTA and competitive performance on UCF-Crime. These results establish coarse video predictions as supervision for recovering the fine-grained evidence supporting them, without corresponding fine-grained labels.
  </details>

- **[From Inference to Adaptation: Vision-Language Model Test-Time Adaptation via a Unified Optimal Transport View](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18339)**  `arXiv:2608.18339`  
  _Qi Yu, Zhichen Zeng, Katherine Tieu, Lingjie Chen, Xiyuan Yang, Ruizhong Qiu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.
  </details>

- **[Remote-Sensing City Layout Extraction with MLLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16484)**  `arXiv:2608.16484`  
  _Zigan Zhou, Kai Li, Yupeng Deng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Remote-sensing systems usually describe urban content with detection boxes, semantic masks, or vector boundaries. Such outputs locate classes and support image-plane scoring, yet they do not by themselves constitute an executable layout that retains object identities, typed relations, topology, and regeneration rules. Code-as-City instead casts urban-layout extraction from a single top-down image as constrained code generation with a multimodal large language model (MLLM). An image model first produces an aligned five-class semantic layout prior. Three ordered MLLM passes use the image and this prior to recover roads, land-cover regions and relations, and buildings. Deterministic normalization converts the accumulated records into a city graph and a restricted layout program. Executing the program creates a renderable 3D city layout and an orthographic semantic projection over shared geometry. The projection admits pixel-level comparison with remote-sensing masks, while named objects, relations, and editing operations remain available for synchronized regeneration of both views. Evaluated on the 100 scenes of CityLayout-100, the complete framework obtains 41.1% mean intersection-over-union and 48.3% global intersection-over-union. This result provides quantitative evidence that visual observations can be translated into inspectable, editable city code with coupled planar and 3D outputs.
  </details>

- **[Unleashing the Potential of Vision-Language Models for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04935)**  `arXiv:2608.04935`  
  _Weihan Cai, Hao Tan, Zichang Tan, Jun Wan, Xinping Gao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A linear classifier trained on frozen DINOv3 features can outperform specialized detectors of AI-generated images in the wild. This success has motivated efforts to further adapt DINOv3 for detection, but we find that the same evaluation protocol underestimates the potential of a vision-language model. When linear probes are trained on images from the same generator, Perception Encoder (PE) performs worse than DINOv3 on in-the-wild benchmarks. Yet real and generated images form more distinct local groups in PE's frozen feature space. Image-text pretraining gives PE a source of supervision directly relevant to this distinction: captions can identify an image as AI-generated, allowing PE to learn high-level semantics about image provenance. Conventional linear probing uses only the image encoder. We introduce Semantic Prototype Calibration (SPC), which instead initializes the linear head of the frozen image encoder with text embeddings that describe real and AI-generated images. Across nine in-the-wild subsets, SPC raises mean accuracy from 84.8\% to 92.9\% for PE and from 81.4\% to 98.5\% for MoEViE. Both models also improve on controlled benchmarks. MoEViE-SPC outperforms specialized detectors with more elaborate task-specific designs. These results establish SPC as a simple and effective baseline for generalizable AI-generated image detection.
  </details>

- **[UniWorld-View: Large-Baseline View Synthesis via Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04701)**  `arXiv:2608.04701`  
  _Wangbo Yu, Haiyang Zhou, Chaoran Feng, Xunyu Zhou, Li Yuan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Novel view synthesis from casually captured monocular images and videos offers a practical route to immersive content creation without dedicated multi-view capture. However, the limited viewpoint coverage of such inputs leaves scene geometry insufficiently constrained, restricting the ability of reconstruction-based methods, such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), to render views far from the observed viewpoints. Generative approaches leverage learned visual priors to synthesize unobserved content, but maintaining geometric consistency and precise camera control remains challenging under large viewpoint changes. We present UniView, a unified framework for large-baseline novel view synthesis and scene generation from monocular images and videos. Central to our approach are an occlusion-aware point cloud renderer and a dual-branch conditioning mechanism. The renderer uses triple reprojection to identify and filter unreliable projections under large viewpoint changes. The conditioning mechanism integrates the resulting geometric guidance with source-view appearance within the video diffusion model, enabling precise camera control while preserving visual details and synthesizing unobserved content. To extend view synthesis to scene generation, we introduce a two-stage generation strategy that decouples viewpoint changes from temporal evolution. This strategy produces dense, synchronized multi-view videos that provide additional supervision for dynamic Gaussian Splatting, enabling more complete 4D generation from monocular observations. Extensive evaluations across static and dynamic scenes demonstrate the effectiveness of UniView in novel view synthesis and scene generation, combining precise camera control with geometric consistency and visual fidelity.
  </details>

- **[When Extreme Darkness Meets Motion Blur: MeanFlow for Unified RAW Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01720)**  `arXiv:2608.01720`  
  _Zepu Wang, Jingze Liang, Weijie Xiao, Kexin Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Extremely low-light RAW enhancement aims to recover severely attenuated sensor signals, yet existing methods often focus on illumination and noise while overlooking the motion-induced degradations inherent in practical low-light imaging. We present a framework for robust extremely low-light RAW enhancement under realistic acquisition degradations. First, we introduce See in the Degraded Extremely Dark (SIDED), a new dataset that applies controlled motion degradation to extremely low-light RAW pairs while retaining their original sensor noise. Second, we propose a unified RAW tokenizer equipped with explicit domain-conditioned representation calibration to align extremely low-light and well-exposed RAW data, followed by a MeanFlow that performs enhancement in a single function evaluation. To our knowledge, this is the first work to formulate extremely low-light RAW enhancement under realistic motion-degraded acquisition and address it with MeanFlow. We further introduce a physics-guided refinement model to strengthen illumination--reflectance consistency, pixel fidelity, and color preservation without incurring additional inference cost. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in extremely low-light RAW enhancement, and robustly handles coupled motion and noise degradations.
  </details>

- **[Which Modality Decides? Counterfactual Modality Attribution for Multimodal Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00076)**  `arXiv:2608.00076`  
  _Vahidin Hasic, Chao Wang, Luis C. Garcia-Peraza-Herrera, David Watson, Senka Krivic_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal classifiers can achieve high accuracy while exploiting modality-specific shortcuts. Modality attribution quantifies the contributions of image and text, but does not by itself identify which input changes would alter a suspicious prediction. We introduce Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), which connects modality-level contributions to explicit prediction-changing edits. CMA uses image and text diffusion priors to generate counterfactual references and constructs a two-player reference game whose Shapley--Taylor decomposition separates image, text, and interaction contributions. The method requires class-score queries but no model gradients. Attribution profiles are compared with a reference population to prioritize predictions with atypical modality reliance for review, while counterfactual edits expose localized evidence for inspection. On controlled image- and text-biased classifiers, CMA identifies the ground truth dominant modality for all evaluated inputs. On planted-shortcut benchmarks, it achieves shortcut-reliance detection AUROCs of 0.987 on Synthetic MNIST and 1.000 on OpenI, with image-shortcut localization IoUs of 0.97 and 0.84, respectively. An API experiment demonstrates applicability to a native multimodal language model with scored answer choices. CMA enables predictions to be screened by modality reliance and investigated through explicit counterfactual edits.
  </details>

- **[PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable Remote Heart Rate Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00066)**  `arXiv:2608.00066`  
  _Yehui Yang, Bo Zhao, Junzhe Cao, Hui Ma, Yue Sun, Wenjin Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos, but its weak physiological signal is easily corrupted by motion, illumination changes, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. Existing rPPG methods typically rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, while different strong estimators may produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video. To resolve these conflicts, we propose PhysAgent, an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework. Unlike direct prediction approaches, PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to output heart rate directly. In contrast, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified and uses a lightweight 4B MLLM, Qwen3-VL-4B, to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate. Experimental results on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show that PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion. The code will be released soon.
  </details>

- **[Training-Free Entity-Level Few-Shot Segmentation of Remote Sensing Images with Advection Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29278)**  `arXiv:2607.29278`  
  _Xueting Bai, Huan Ni_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing cross-domain few-shot segmentation approaches suffer from high training costs due to source-domain episodic training and pixel-wise dense prediction, while often producing fragmented and noisy predictions in remote sensing images. To overcome these issues, we propose ELFSS-AR, a training-free entity-level few-shot segmentation method with advection refinement. Specifically, ELFSS-AR first leverages SAM3's generic geometric priors to generate category-agnostic entity primitives, and reformulates few-shot inference from pixel-level prediction to entity-level reasoning. Subsequently, foreground and background prototypes are constructed and combined with dense textual semantic responses from SAM3 to build a multi-modal semantic potential field. An advection equation-based semantic refinement mechanism is then introduced to propagate category-aware information across both feature and multi-source response spaces, further enhancing semantic continuity and suppressing local texture noise. Extensive experiments on multiple remote sensing datasets demonstrate that ELFSS-AR effectively mitigates domain shift and local noise, substantially improving SAM3's adaptation capability for remote sensing few-shot segmentation without additional training. The code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[FreqForcing: Autoregressive Long Video Generation via Spectral Self-Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27110)**  `arXiv:2607.27110`  
  _Jiatong Li, Yulun Zhang, Leo Liang, Linghe Kong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autoregressive video diffusion models enable real-time streaming video generation. However, errors introduced during self-rollout accumulate over long horizons, manifesting as color drift, motion stagnation, and eventual visual collapse. Existing training-free methods attribute error accumulation to the loss of historical context and use attention sink to compensate for this loss. However, we find that visual degradation primarily stems from erroneous historical tokens, whose key-value pairs distort attention outputs. Although attention sink partially alleviates this issue, visual degradation persists. Motivated by the above analysis, we propose FreqForcing, a training-free framework that rectifies attention outputs in long-video generation via Spectral Self-Anchoring (SSA). The proposed SSA leverages the low-frequency components of anchor attention to maintain long-horizon visual stability, while preserving recent changes through the high-frequency components of local attention. FreqForcing extends models pretrained on 5s clips to minutes-long generation without finetuning. Extensive experiments show that FreqForcing outperforms existing training-free methods quantitatively and qualitatively.
  </details>

- **[The generator is the tracker: Multi-object tracking by painting persistent identity colours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17120)**  `arXiv:2607.17120`  
  _Haiyu Yang, Miel Hostens_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-object tracking (MOT) is usually split into detection and association, with identity kept as external state: track buffers, motion models, appearance embeddings. We ask whether a video generator can keep that state in pixels. We fine-tune a 22B text-to-video diffusion model (LTX-2.3) with an in-context LoRA to translate an RGB clip into an ID-map clip, where every person is painted a flat, distinct colour that persists over time. Long videos are generated as chained windows, each conditioned on the cleaned tail of the previous one; a brief continuation fine-tune teaches the model to extend a given colouring, after which identity flows through the chain with no separately trained detector, motion model or association module. On the DanceTrack test server the system reaches 40.3 HOTA, to our knowledge the first entry read off a pretrained video generator. This is well below today's specialists (66-76 HOTA), but its association (AssA 44.1) exceeds every tracker of the 2020-22 benchmark suite while detection is the deficit. A 2x2 factorial on validation shows where identity comes from: neither chaining nor continuation training helps alone (16.8 and 15.9 HOTA against 18.2 for independent windows linked post hoc), but together they reach 34.8; re-linking the chain's own windows changes nothing (34.7), and motion- and appearance-based associators on the same boxes reach only 22-24 AssA against 38.3 for the colours, an ordering that holds in three sampling seeds and on SportsMOT. On 383 mined occlusion and exit events the chain re-acquires 42% of the identities it held on both sides of the gap, including gaps longer than its 49-frame context; the pre-gap colour is painted during the gap in every recovery but also in 110 of 119 failures, so carry-over is necessary but not sufficient. We offer the system as a proof of concept, not a competitive tracker. We release code and checkpoints.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Single Expert: Harmonizing Diverse Visual Priors in MLLMs for Spatial Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15054)**  `arXiv:2607.15054`  
  _Xiao Lin, Xiaohu Huang, Kai Han_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated substantial promise in spatial understanding. Existing works typically incorporate prior knowledge extracted from a pre-trained foundation model to further enhance the spatial awareness of MLLMs. In this paper, we first reveal that when integrating diverse foundation models into MLLMs, different models provide complementary spatial priors that benefit different tasks. Motivated by this, we propose $\textbf{ViPS}$, a novel multi-model prior framework designed to fully unleash the potential of incorporating multiple $\textbf{Vi}$sual $\textbf{P}$riors from diverse models into MLLMs for $\textbf{S}$patial understanding. Specifically, ViPS introduces an Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism to achieve harmonious and context-aware prior fusion and injection from the prior proxies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViPS successfully harmonizes diverse visual priors, establishing new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.03836)**  `arXiv:2607.03836`  
  _Nguyen Kim Hai Bui, Md. Easin Arafat, Tamás Gábor Orosz, Mufti Mahmud_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.
  </details>

- **[Absorption-Feature-Guided Distance-Decoupled Estimation and Band Selection for LWIR Hyperspectral Passive Ranging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31824)**  `arXiv:2606.31824`  
  _Shuo Liu, Chen Fan, Zhihe Chen, Xiaolin Huang, Lilian Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In long-wave infrared (LWIR) hyperspectral observations, atmospheric absorption imprints distance-dependent spectral signatures on observed radiance, enabling passive ranging. However, these signatures are nonlinearly coupled with target temperature, material emissivity, and path radiance, making distance inversion ill-posed. Existing methods rely on full-band measurements and pixel-wise joint optimization of distance, temperature, and emissivity, resulting in high computational cost. We propose an Absorption-Guided Distance-Decoupled Estimation and Refinement (ADER) framework that exploits sharp atmospheric absorption structures for efficient ranging. ADER represents material emissivity with B-spline control points under a spectral-smoothness prior to suppress overfitting to absorption structures. Using ozone-absorption cues to identify reflected downwelling radiance, ADER classifies pixels as emission-dominant or reflection-dominant. For emission-dominant pixels, it compensates for path radiance and transmittance and estimates distance by one-dimensional minimization of an absorption residual. For reflection-dominant pixels, it refines the initial estimate using the complete radiative model with downwelling-radiance compensation. A greedy band selection strategy based on multi-scene effective Fisher information reduces spectral redundancy while preserving distance information. Real-scene experiments show that, in a representative LiDAR-referenced grass region, full-band and 20-band ADER yield mean distance deviations of 0.20 m and 0.40 m from LiDAR, respectively, and achieve approximately 130x and 179x speedups over the reproduced hyperspectral baseline.
  </details>

- **[MuseBench: Benchmarking Intent-Level Audiovisual Arts Understanding in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30026)**  `arXiv:2606.30026`  
  _Yuxuan Fan, Gyusik Seo, Jing Hao, Jaemin Cho, Mohit Bansal, Jaehong Yoon_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Audiovisual arts encompass diverse creative disciplines, including cinema, visual arts, stage performance, and game design, where artistic meaning arises from deliberate combinations of visual, auditory, and narrative elements (e.g., fear amplified through claustrophobic framing, or grief conveyed through silence and lingering close-ups). Artistic understanding extends beyond recognizing what is depicted to reasoning about why it is expressed through particular creative choices. Despite progress in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), reasoning about artistic intent remains underexplored, as existing benchmarks largely measure perceptual recognition. To address this gap, we introduce MuseBench, a benchmark for evaluating intent-level artistic understanding in MLLMs. It comprises 4,016 questions derived from video essays spanning cinematic arts, static visual arts, stage performing arts, and game arts. To capture the open-ended nature of artistic analysis at scale, the benchmark combines single-select and variable-option multi-select questions. All questions are generated and refined through a four-phase iterative pipeline combining shortcut filtering, adversarial distractors, and expert validation. We evaluate 34 MLLM versions using either video and audio transcripts (V+T) or video, native audio, and text (V+A+T). The highest observed accuracy is 64.62% (V+A+T), trailing the 87.18% human expert baseline. Further analysis reveals that native-audio models score lowest on game arts, models often recover partial interpretations but struggle to identify complete correct option sets on multi-select items, and adaptive frame-selection models trail the strongest video-specific model. These results identify artistic knowledge and complete interpretation as challenges for audiovisual models.
  </details>

- **[T-VSS: Test-Time Visual Subspace Steering for Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23132)**  `arXiv:2606.23132`  
  _Jaehyuk Jang, Minseok Seo, Seungju Cho, Kangwook Ko, Changick Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs), exemplified by CLIP, enable strong zero-shot visual recognition but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Recent test-time adaptation methods improve robustness without retraining. Prompt-based methods adapt learnable text prompts, while input-space methods optimize pixels or padding at test time. These approaches can improve predictions, but they do so through an indirect and expensive optimization path. We propose \textbf{Test-time Visual Subspace Steering (T-VSS)}, a lightweight defense that performs test-time adaptation directly in the visual feature space. T-VSS first builds a sample-specific low-rank subspace from multi-view feature residuals anchored at the attacked image. It then learns a shared feature correction within this subspace using reliability-weighted entropy minimization. By constraining adaptation to a compact visual geometry, T-VSS steers attacked features toward more stable and discriminative predictions while avoiding noisy full-space updates. Experiments on fine-grained, ImageNet, and ImageNet-OOD benchmarks show that T-VSS improves adversarial robustness while maintaining competitive clean accuracy and better efficiency than prior test-time adaptation methods. Code is available at \href{this https URL}{here}.
  </details>

- **[NAMESAKES: Probing Identity Memorization in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20155)**  `arXiv:2606.20155`  
  _Morris Alper, Vasudha Varadarajan, Moran Yanuka, Angelina Wang, Hadar Averbuch-Elor_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-image (T2I) models generate realistic likenesses of some individuals when prompted with their names, raising privacy concerns. However, distinguishing whether a generated face is memorized or fabricated currently requires ground-truth photos, access to training data, or white-box access to model internals, limiting applicability. We introduce a fully black-box behavioral probe that distinguishes between memorized and unrecognized names, while requiring no reference photos or prior knowledge of training data. To benchmark this task, we present the NAMESAKES dataset of over one thousand names and faces of public figures spanning a wide range of fame levels, along with perturbed, less famous names. Experiments on state-of-the-art T2I models show that our probe substantially predicts identity memorization and separates memorized from unrecognized names, with further insights into differences across model families.
  </details>

- **[From Context to Canvas: Benchmark Dataset and Verify-then-Route Framework for Multi-Subject Reference-Based Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15867)**  `arXiv:2606.15867`  
  _Long-Bao Nguyen, Quang-Khai Le, Tam V. Nguyen, Minh-Triet Tran, Trung-Nghia Le_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Personalized image generation should compose several people, each with the right objects and outfits, in a specified scene, yet current generators collapse as references are added and existing benchmarks do not capture this degradation. We introduce CogCanvas, a benchmark of 1,361 compositional prompts with 2--5 subjects, 1,952 curated references (100 people, 115 objects and fashion items, 29 scenes), and graphs specifying interactions and spatial relations. It adds two metrics: BG-Sim for background fidelity outside foreground regions, and Attr-VQA for person--item binding, with 76.5% agreement with human majority judgments. We also propose Context2Canvas, a training-free multi-agent framework built on a verify-then-route principle: agents verify a layout against a hierarchical scene graph, and its masks then route each reference to its own region in a two-phase renderer that grounds references independently before refining them jointly. Context2Canvas achieves 2.5x the attribute-binding score of the strongest published baseline, with larger gains as the subject count increases. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[AVIS: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11576)**  `arXiv:2606.11576`  
  _Ahmadreza Jeddi, Minh Ngoc Le, Amirhossein Kazerouni, Hakki Can Karaimer, Hue Nguyen, Iqbal Mohomed, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) benefit from chain-of-thought prompting and test-time scaling, but these gains often come with prohibitive inference cost due to large visual contexts and long decoding chains. We view this cost through two coupled axes: Visual Context Scaling (VCS), which controls how much visual evidence is passed to the language model, and Visual Reasoning Scaling (VRS), which controls how much inference-time reasoning search is performed. Existing methods typically optimize one axis at a time, leaving the joint allocation of compute across these axes underexplored. We introduce Adaptive Visual Inference Scaling (AVIS), a lightweight policy that adapts both VCS and VRS per query. AVIS realizes VCS through Key Diversity Visual (KDV) pruning, a training-free $O(N)$ key-based rule for removing redundant visual tokens before prefilling, and realizes VRS through adaptive self-consistency, using a learned difficulty predictor to select the number of reasoning rollouts. AVIS is deployment-friendly and compatible with shared-prefill inference, where all rollouts reuse a single prefilling pass and KV cache. Across diverse image and video reasoning benchmarks, AVIS improves the accuracy--compute trade-off relative to VCS-only and VRS-only baselines, and remains effective on top of RL post-trained VLMs while keeping compute and latency low.
  </details>

- **[Let It Be Simple: One-Step Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05737)**  `arXiv:2606.05737`  
  _Yitong Chen, Shiduo Zhang, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  One-step generation from standard diffusion or Flow-Matching training is rarely effective for text-to-image or video generation without distillation or specialized one-step objectives. We find that VLA action generation behaves strikingly differently. Biasing only the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong one-step policies across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and real-world robot tasks. Moreover, for open-source VLA models with different architectures, simply replacing iterative decoding with a single forward pass often performs comparably to the original multi-step decoding on benchmarks such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv. We attribute this difference to the condition-target structure of VLA generation, which is closer to image-to-text than text-to-image: rich observations strongly constrain a comparatively compact target. We formalize this intuition through the irreducible velocity loss $R_v(t,c)$ of standard Flow Matching, which becomes much smaller toward the noise endpoint for VLA, whereas image-generation models usually exhibit a U-shaped profile. The geometry induced by the learned generative map shows the same contrast: the Jacobian of this map with respect to the initial noise has a substantially smaller largest singular value for action generation than for image generation. Together, these results suggest that VLA's condition-target structure makes one-step generation unusually accessible to standard Flow Matching. Code and training configurations for this paper are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Smooth Inliers, Erratic Outliers: Frequency-Aware Mamba for Two-View Correspondence Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04493)**  `arXiv:2606.04493`  
  _Zhihua Wang, Yifeng Gao, Yunhao Feng, Rui Pan, Zhouyuan Ma, Baiheng Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When shown matches between two photographs of the same cathedral, people can tell at a glance which ones are wrong: a window matched to its look-alike jumps against its neighbors, while correct matches shift together. Two-view correspondence learning, also called correspondence pruning, asks a network to make this judgment for thousands of candidate matches, most of which are wrong. Mamba, a fast sequence model, now drives strong pruners, but it reads the matches as a plain sequence, and whether its scan can capture such agreement is unclear. We propose SFMambaNet, which scans the matches cluster by cluster, so that correct matches vary slowly along the sequence while wrong ones stay erratic, and filters the scanned features with learnable frequency-domain gates between its forward and backward passes. On camera pose estimation, outlier removal and homography estimation, we find that SFMambaNet outperforms spatial-domain Mamba baselines with about two million parameters. Contrary to the usual expectation that such gains come from extra capacity, we find that a parameter-free low-pass filter beats point-wise layers as large as the gates. The learned gates turn low-pass on their own and make the scan far less sensitive to how the matches are shuffled. Together, these results show that frequency is a natural language for describing agreement between correspondences, with implications for other sequence models that must read unordered sets, such as point clouds and graphs.
  </details>

- **[FlatVPR: Plug-and-play Geo-linear Residual Adapter for Geometric Rectification of Foundation Model Feature Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01734)**  `arXiv:2606.01734`  
  _Rai Hisada, Kanji Tanaka_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper proposes ``FlatVPR,'' a novel geometric rectification paradigm that effectively bridges the trade-off between map lightweightness and localization accuracy in visual place recognition (VPR) by enforcing a feature manifold structure where any descriptor between two adjacent anchors $\mathbf{z}_A$ and $\mathbf{z}_B$ can be accurately reconstructed via linear interpolation $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{pseudo} = (1-t)\mathbf{z}_A + t\mathbf{z}_B$, where $t \in [0,1]$ denotes the relative position. While state-of-the-art foundation models such as DINOv2-ViT-S/14 provide robust semantic features, their latent manifolds exhibit prominent curvature, projecting uniform linear motion in physical space onto highly non-linear trajectories in the feature space, which hinders reliable reconstruction under sparse anchor conditions. To enable the aforementioned interpolation-based reconstruction, we introduce a residual transformation $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{z} + \text{Res}(\mathbf{z})$ to the raw foundation features $\mathbf{z}$, where $\text{Res}(\cdot)$ represents a learnable adapter. Our method explicitly suppresses manifold curvature using a mathematically grounded Pullback Flatness Loss that minimizes the deviation of intermediate features from the linear segment connecting adjacent anchors, thereby minimizing the intrinsic curvature of the manifold. Through this spatial flattening, map construction is formulated within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework, decoupled into a continuous M-step for manifold adaptation and a conceptual E-step for optimal anchor selection guidelines. Experiments on the NCLT dataset demonstrate that the application of our adapter leads to significant performance improvements even under extremely sparse anchor conditions with 100m intervals and extreme seasonal changes.
  </details>

- **[ChartArena: A Unified Benchmark with Atomic-Primitive Reasoning for Chart Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01348)**  `arXiv:2606.01348`  
  _Shangpin Peng, Gengluo Li, Xingyu Wan, Chengquan Zhang, Hao Feng, Binghong Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Charts convey dense quantitative and relational information, yet current general chart parsing remains challenging due to fragmented evaluation and limited structural reasoning. Existing benchmarks focus on narrow sub-tasks with inconsistent output formats (e.g., Markdown, CSV, JSON, SVG, code), hindering fair comparison and often overlooking real-world scenarios such as printed or hand-drawn photos. Meanwhile, end-to-end multimodal models tend to learn shallow pixel-to-text mappings without explicit structure understanding, making them fragile under visual variations. To address these issues, we present a unified framework that connects evaluation and modeling. On the evaluation side, we introduce ChartArena, a comprehensive bilingual benchmark covering eight chart families, including both numeric charts (bar, line, pie, radar, box plot, combination) and diagrammatic structures (flowchart, mind map). The dataset is constructed via a human-agent collaborative annotation pipeline, where model-assisted drafts are refined through multi-stage human verification to ensure structural consistency and annotation reliability. Furthermore, we design a format-agnostic evaluation protocol that maps different outputs into two canonical semantic spaces: a normalized triple view and a directed graph view, and evaluates them with structure-aware metrics. On the modeling side, we propose Chart Atomic Primitives (CAP), a lightweight semantic scaffold that introduces structural inductive bias during supervised fine-tuning. By guiding the model to infer structure before generating outputs, CAP leads to more consistent and robust parsing behavior. Extensive experiments show that models trained with CAP mechanism achieve reliable performance on ChartArena. ChartArena is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[PARE: Pruning and Adaptive Routing for Efficient Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27336)**  `arXiv:2605.27336`  
  _Yutong Wang, Yunke Wang, Tianfan Xue, Yu Qiao, Yaohui Wang, Xinyuan Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) generate high-quality videos but demand substantial compute due to wide blocks, deep architectures, and iterative sampling. Recent methods reduce cost by compressing width, depth, or sampling steps, but typically commit to a fixed architecture that cannot adapt to individual inputs or denoising stages. We propose PARE (Pruning and Adaptive Routing for Efficient video generation), which jointly compresses width and depth with structure-aware pruning and input-adaptive routing. For width, we observe that attention heads specialize into spatial and temporal roles, and design importance scoring that accounts for this distinction to prevent motion-critical temporal heads from being pruned prematurely. For depth, we train a lightweight router conditioned on denoising timestep and visual content to dynamically select which blocks to execute at each step, enabling per-input compute adaptation rather than static block removal. A progressive pipeline first recovers width-pruned quality via distillation, then jointly optimizes the student and router to decouple the two learning objectives. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B for both image-to-video and text-to-video generation show that PARE substantially reduces per-step computation while preserving quality across VBench dimensions, and composes with step distillation for further acceleration.
  </details>

- **[Pop-Up Distractions Reveal Bag-of-Events Behavior in Video Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27101)**  `arXiv:2605.27101`  
  _Oscar Chew, Serhii Honcharenko, Qian-Hui Chen, Patricia Lu, Dishant Zaveri, Khoa D. Doan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A key capability for video understanding is reliably linking subjects to events across time, yet whether Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) actually achieve this remains unclear. In this work, we introduce DistractionBench to evaluate whether VideoLLMs can robustly link subjects and events in the presence of unrelated video segments. Through controlled interventions, such as inserting short advertisement clips into longer videos, we show that VideoLLMs frequently hallucinate interactions between entities from different segments, incorrectly attributing actions from injected advertisements to subjects in the main video. We characterize this systematic hallucination as bag-of-events (BoE) behavior, where models process videos as collections of events rather than temporally structured sequences. Evaluating 11 popular VideoLLMs, we find that all models exhibit substantial BoE behavior. Our findings suggest that VideoLLMs lack reliable mechanisms for temporal grounding and motivate the development of models with more robust subject-event association.
  </details>

- **[LaMo: Self-Supervised Latent Motion Priors for Physical Realism in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23878)**  `arXiv:2605.23878`  
  _Bo Jiang, Depu Meng, Yihan Hu, Yichen Xie, Tianshuo Xu, Wei Zhan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern video generators produce visually compelling clips but still struggle with physical and motion consistency, limiting their use as reliable world simulators. Existing remedies often rely on external simulators, teacher models, or curated physics-focused data. We explore a complementary self-supervised direction: extracting motion cues from the unlabeled videos already used to train video diffusion models. We propose LaMo, which formulates a latent motion prior over frame-to-frame latent changes conditioned on the current latent and prompt. This prior is exposed through two lightweight readouts: a macro motion drift used during training as a Motion Drift Loss, and a learned micro motion field used during sampling as Motion Prior Guidance. Both components are plug-and-play with existing video diffusion backbones, requiring no architectural or I/O changes. On VideoPhy, VideoPhy2, and PisaBench, LaMo improves CogVideoX backbones and outperforms recent physics-aware baselines that use external supervision. On VBench, it preserves overall generation quality while improving motion-related dimensions. These results suggest that unlabeled video contains useful motion supervision for improving physical fidelity in modern video diffusion models.
  </details>

- **[GRTO: Group Relative Tool Optimization for Referring Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23500)**  `arXiv:2605.23500`  
  _Mario Markov, Stefan Maria Ailuro, Mohammad Mahdi, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Referring segmentation requires reasoning to connect language with visual evidence and identify the intended target in challenging scenarios. This makes GRPO a natural choice for training VLMs together with a segmentation tool. However, existing approaches optimize only the VLM, assuming that the tool is perfect and leaving it untouched. This assumption is particularly limiting when the tool faces domain shift, as segmentation errors can undermine even correct reasoning. We therefore argue that the segmentation tool should be optimized together with the reasoning policy. However, this is challenging because policy optimization and differentiable tool learning rely on fundamentally different objectives. In this work, we introduce group relative tool optimization (GRTO), a mathematically grounded two-stage framework for jointly optimizing a policy and its differentiable tool. The key idea is to first align the tool with the policy expected after joint training, rather than the initial policy. The prealigned tool then leads to a more robust reward signal and superior policy convergence in subsequent policy training. In the first stage, GRTO bootstraps the tool toward the theoretically optimal policy, capturing readily attainable gains without costly on-policy rollouts. This alignment bootstraps the second stage, where GRTO extends GRPO to jointly refine the policy and tool. Across three challenging referring segmentation benchmarks, GRTO achieves substantial improvements over plain GRPO and alternative tool training procedures, matching or surpassing domain-specific state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates the value of unifying reinforcement learning with differentiable auxiliary objectives for reasoning-intensive segmentation.
  </details>

- **[Aligning Network Equivariance with Data Symmetry: A Theoretical Framework and Adaptive Approach for Image Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13744)**  `arXiv:2605.13744`  
  _Feiyu Tan, Qi Xie, Zongben Xu, Deyu Meng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image restoration is an inherently ill posed inverse problem. Equivariant networks that embed geometric symmetry priors can mitigate this ill posedness and improve performance. However, current understanding of the relationship between network equivariance and data symmetry remains largely heuristic. Particularly for real world data with imperfect symmetry, existing research lacks a systematic theoretical framework to quantify symmetry, select transformation groups, or evaluate model data alignment. To bridge this gap, we conduct an analysis from an optimization perspective and formalize the intrinsic relationship among data symmetry priors, model equivariance, and generalization capability. Specifically, we propose for the first time a quantifiable definition of non strict symmetry at the dataset level (rather than sample level) and use it as a constraint to formulate the restoration inverse problem. We then show that the equivariance for restoration models can be naturally derived from this inverse problems incorporated the proposed symmetry constraints, and that the equivariance error of the optimal restoration operator is strictly bounded by the data symmetry error and the discretization mesh size. Furthermore, by analyzing the network's empirical risk, we demonstrate that aligning equivariance with data symmetry optimizes the bias variance trade off, minimizing the total expected risk. Guided by these insights, we propose a Sample Adaptive Equivariant Network that uses a hypernetwork and transformation learnable equivariant convolutions to dynamically align with each sample's inherent symmetry. Extensive experiments on super resolution, denoising, and deraining validate our theoretical findings and show significant superiority over standard baselines and traditional equivariant models. Our code and supplementary material are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[SCALER: Breaking the Latent Scaling Bottleneck via Single-Pass Context-Anchored Latent Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12163)**  `arXiv:2605.12163`  
  _Chenfeng Wang, Wei Zhai, Wei He, Xuhan Zhu, Chunpeng Zhou, Song Yan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Longer chains of thought substantially improve language reasoning on complex problems, inspiring efforts to scale visual reasoning via continuous latents. However, evaluating visual latent reasoning across complexity and sequence length reveals a fundamental **Latent Scaling Bottleneck**: existing methods yield modest gains only within short budgets ($\leq 30$ tokens) on simple tasks, yet stagnate or *degrade* on harder tasks and longer chains. Controlled diagnostics trace this bottleneck to two root causes. First, **Latent Representation Saturation** under autoregressive conditioning causes step-wise cosine novelty to decay exponentially and saturate after $\sim 30$ steps. Second, **Over-Compressed Supervision Targets** from heavily pooled ($\geq 128\times$) image embeddings lose fine-grained spatial structure and act like meaningless padding. We propose **SCALER** (**S**ingle-Pass **C**ontext-**A**nchored **L**at**e**nt Visual **R**easoning), whose lightweight *detransformer* synthesizes spatially aligned auxiliary tokens from full-sequence hidden states *in a single forward pass*, anchoring each token to the original visual space. Coupled with three-stage SFT and **ALPO** (**A**uxiliary **L**atent **P**olicy **O**ptimization) for differentiable RL, SCALER extends effective latent length by over $30\times$, achieves state-of-the-art open-source accuracy (e.g., **57.84%** on MME-RealWorld-Lite, +12.09% over backbone, +10.47% over GPT-6-luna), with strong OOD generalization. Our project page: [this https URL](this https URL).
  </details>

- **[Common Principal Component Networks for Domain Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05136)**  `arXiv:2605.05136`  
  _Yu-Hsi Chen, Abd-Krim Seghouane_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Domain Generalization (DG) aims to learn representations that generalize to unseen target domains under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. Despite recent advances in invariant representation learning, explicitly capturing shared structures across source-domain distributions remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we integrate Common Principal Component Analysis (CPCA) into deep learning to identify a common orthogonal basis across multiple domains, proposing two complementary end-to-end differentiable frameworks. First, we introduce Common Principal Component Network (CPCNet), which unrolls the iterative Flury-Gautschi (FG) algorithm into fully differentiable neural layers, enabling covariance-based joint diagonalization within end-to-end representation learning. Second, to address rank deficiency arising from mini-batch covariance estimation in small-sample regimes, we develop Projection Pursuit-based Common Principal Component Network (PP-CPCNet), which directly optimizes a common orthogonal basis without explicit covariance estimation. Experiments validate the joint diagonalization capabilities of both methods, while evaluations on four standard DG benchmarks demonstrate competitive zero-shot generalization performance with favorable computational efficiency.
  </details>

- **[NucEval: Revisiting and Extending Evaluation Metrics for Nuclear Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03144)**  `arXiv:2605.03144`  
  _Amirreza Mahbod, Ramona Woitek, Jeanne Shen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In computational pathology, nuclear instance segmentation is a fundamental task with many downstream clinical applications. With the advent of deep learning, many approaches, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs), have been proposed for this task, along with both machine learning-based and non-machine learning-based pre- and post-processing techniques to further boost performance. However, one fundamental aspect that has received less attention is the evaluation pipeline. In this study, we identify four key issues associated with nuclear instance segmentation evaluation and propose corresponding solutions. Our proposed modifications, namely handling vague regions, score normalization, overlapping instances, and border uncertainty, are integrated into a unified framework called NucEval, which extends commonly used metrics for evaluating nuclear instance segmentation. We evaluate this framework on the NuInsSeg dataset, which provides unique characteristics that make it particularly suitable for this study, as well as two additional external datasets, using three CNN- and ViT-based nuclear instance segmentation models. Beyond its effect on the metrics, we show that NucEval increases inter- and intra-observer agreement between expert annotations and can change the ranking of closely competing methods on an external benchmark, indicating that the choice of evaluation protocol can affect model selection. The code, along with complete guidelines and illustrative examples, is publicly available at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[TT4D: A Pipeline and Dataset for Table Tennis 4D Reconstruction From Monocular Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01234)**  `arXiv:2605.01234`  
  _Nima Rahmanian, Daniel Kienzle, Thomas Gossard, Dvij Kalaria, Rainer Lienhart, Shankar Sastry_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present TT4D, a large-scale, high-fidelity table tennis dataset. It provides $140+$ hours of reconstructed singles and doubles gameplay from monocular broadcast videos, featuring multimodal annotations like high-quality camera calibrations, precise 3D ball positions, ball spin, time segmentation, and 3D human meshes over time. This rich data provides a new foundation for virtual replay, in-depth player analysis, and robot learning. The dataset's combination of scale and precision is achieved through a novel reconstruction pipeline. Prior methods first partition a game sequence into individual shot segments based on the 2D ball track, and only then attempt reconstruction. However, 2D-based time segmentation collapses under occlusion and varied camera viewpoints, preventing reliable reconstruction. We invert this paradigm by first lifting the entire unsegmented 2D ball track to 3D through a learned lifting network. This 3D trajectory then allows us to reliably perform time segmentation. The learned lifting network also infers the ball's spin, handles unreliable ball detections, and successfully reconstructs the ball trajectory in cases of high occlusion. This lift-first design is necessary, as our pipeline is the only method capable of reconstructing table tennis gameplay from general-view broadcast monocular videos. We demonstrate the dataset's fidelity through two downstream tasks: estimating the racket's pose \& velocity at impact, and training a generative model of competitive rallies.
  </details>

- **[Faithful Extreme Image Rescaling with Learnable Reversible Transformation and Semantic Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00605)**  `arXiv:2605.00605`  
  _Hao Wei, Yanhui Zhou, Chenyang Ge, Saeed Anwar, Ajmal Mian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Most recent extreme rescaling methods struggle to preserve semantically consistent structures and produce realistic details, due to the severely ill-posed nature of low- to high-resolution mapping under scaling factors of $16\times$ or higher. To alleviate the above problems, we propose FaithEIR, a diffusion-based framework for extreme image rescaling. Our code, model weights, and detailed results are released atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Beyond SFT-to-RL: Pre-alignment via Black-Box On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28123)**  `arXiv:2604.28123`

Our code, data, and model checkpoints are publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[MemOVCD: Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Change Detection via Cross-Temporal Memory Reasoning and Global-Local Adaptive Rectification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26774)**  `arXiv:2604.26774`  
  _Zuzheng Kuang, Honghao Chang, Boqiang Liang, Haoqian Wang, Lijun He, Fan Li, et al._

  Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) seeks to identify semantic changes in bi-temporal remote sensing imagery with text-specified target categories. Specifically, MemOVCD casts bi-temporal analysis as a bidirectional two-frame tracking problem and exploits the memory mechanism of video SAM to propagate semantic candidate regions across timestamps. Subsequently, a shared memory, whose number of prototypes is determined by local-exemplar availability, aggregates regional features from the unlabeled target collection. We further devise a global-local adaptive rectification strategy, which adaptively fuses local and global predictions to compensate for incomplete spatial support when processing large images while preserving fine-grained details.   </details>

- **[Conditional Evidence Reconstruction and Decomposition for Interpretable Multimodal Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17030)**  `arXiv:2604.17030`  
  _Shaowen Wan, Bowen Chen, Yanjun Lv, Lu Zhang, Dajiang Zhu, Bharat Biswal, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

However, in both large-scale cohorts and real-world clinical workflows, modality coverage is often incomplete, making many multimodal models brittle when one or more modalities are unavailable. Existing approaches to incomplete multimodal diagnosis typically rely on group-wise or static priors, which may fail to capture subject-specific cross-modal dependencies; moreover, many models provide limited interpretability into which evidence sources drive the final decision. To address these limitations, we propose Conditional Evidence Reconstruction and Decomposition (CERD), a framework for interpretable multimodal diagnosis with incomplete modalities. CERD first reconstructs missing modality representations conditioned on each subject's observed inputs, then decomposes diagnostic evidence into shared cross-modal corroboration and modality-specific cues via logit-level attribution.   </details>

- **[Early-Fusion Cue Analysis for Thin-Obstacle Semantic Segmentation in UAV Navigation: A Systematic Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09694)**  `arXiv:2604.09694`

Incorporating edges alongside depth yields limited additional benefit, with the effect varying across architectures and obstacle categories. Architecture choice also has a larger influence on inference throughput than the addition of depth or edge channels.
  </details>

- **[MEDIC-AD: Towards Medical Vision-Language Model's Clinical Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27176)**  `arXiv:2603.27176`  
  _Woohyeon Park, Jaeik Kim, Sunghwan Steve Cho, Pa Hong, Wookyoung Jeong, Yoojin Nam, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

  </details>

- **[Recurrent Second-Order Learning for Efficient Video Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26134)**  `arXiv:2603.26134`  
  _Jintong Hu, Bin Chen, Zhenyu Hu, Jiayue Liu, Guo Wang, Lu Qi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video super-resolution (VSR) seeks to reconstruct high-resolution frames from low-resolution inputs. While diffusion-based methods have substantially improved perceptual quality, extending them to video remains challenging for two reasons: strong generative priors can introduce temporal instability, and multi-frame diffusion pipelines are often too expensive for practical deployment. To address both challenges simultaneously, we propose InstaVSR, a lightweight diffusion framework for efficient video super-resolution. InstaVSR combines three ingredients: (1) a pruned one-step diffusion backbone that removes several costly components from conventional diffusion-based VSR pipelines, (2) recurrent training with flow-guided temporal regularization to improve frame-to-frame stability, and (3) dual-space adversarial learning in latent and pixel spaces to preserve perceptual quality after backbone simplification. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090, InstaVSR processes a 30-frame video at 2K$\times$2K resolution in under one minute with only 7 GB of memory usage, substantially reducing the computational cost compared to existing diffusion-based methods while maintaining favorable perceptual quality with significantly smoother temporal transitions.
  </details>

- **[Instruction-Free Tuning of Large Vision Language Models for Medical Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19482)**  `arXiv:2603.19482`  
  _Myeongkyun Kang, Soopil Kim, Xiaoxiao Li, Sang Hyun Park_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large vision language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of tasks. These capabilities largely stem from visual instruction tuning, which fine-tunes models on datasets consisting of curated image-instruction-output triplets. However, in the medical domain, constructing large-scale, high-quality instruction datasets is particularly challenging because curation by clinical experts is costly and difficult to scale. To address this issue, we propose an instruction-free tuning approach that reduces reliance on manually curated or generated instructions, leveraging only image-description pairs for fine-tuning. Specifically, we introduce a proxy instruction as a replacement for curated text instructions, which preserves the instruction-following capability of the pre-trained LVLM. By gradually updating the proxy instruction via an exponential moving average, we promote updates to parameters that remain valid during inference. Additionally, we incorporate a response shuffling strategy to mitigate the model's over-reliance on previous words, facilitating more effective fine-tuning. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple-choice visual question answering tasks across SKINCON, WBCAtt, CBIS, and MIMIC-CXR datasets, significantly enhancing the fine-tuning efficiency of LVLMs in medical domains.
  </details>

- **[AGuide: Guiding Air-Ground Feature Adaptation with Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13919)**  `arXiv:2603.13919`  
  _Xianke Wu, Xinyi Li, Minxue Li, Jian Di, Guiyang Luo, Yonglin Tian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Air--ground collaborative perception uses aerial observations to extend vehicle sensing coverage and alleviate occlusion. However, viewpoint differences create a cross-platform representation gap that limits the effective use of aerial information. Existing methods focus on depth estimation, feature interaction, and agent association, with less attention to explicit UAV-to-vehicle feature adaptation. UAV features can be adapted before fusion to bridge this gap, but adapters are typically trained with detection loss alone, which supervises adaptation indirectly through the final predictions. To provide explicit cross-platform supervision, we propose AGuide, a dual-granularity Flow Matching framework that provides explicit cross-platform auxiliary supervision through paired velocity prediction. Both branches learn to predict UAV-to-vehicle feature displacements along interpolation paths, providing directional guidance for UAV adaptation alongside detection supervision. We further introduce OPV2V-Air, a camera-based benchmark for air--ground collaborative perception. AGuide improves AP@0.7 by 2.5 percentage points on OPV2V-Air and 4.0 percentage points on V2U4Real, demonstrating more accurate detection in both camera-based simulation and real-world LiDAR-based collaboration.
  </details>

- **[CT-VDETR: Semi-supervised 3D Trauma Detection in Computed Tomography (CT) scans using Dense Vertex Relative Position Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12514)**  `arXiv:2603.12514`  
  _Shivam Chaudhary, Sheethal Bhat, Andreas Maier_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate detection and localization of traumatic injuries in abdominal CT remain challenging because voxel-level annotations are limited and expensive to obtain. We present a label-efficient framework for 3D abdominal trauma detection that combines self-supervised pretraining with semi-supervised transformer-based detection. First, we use Masked Image Modeling (MIM) on 1,098 CT volumes to pretrain a 3D U-Net encoder for anatomical representation learning. Next, we adapt V-DETR to dense volumetric CT through a feature adapter that converts the encoder feature grid into a compact token sequence for transformer decoding. On this benchmark, the proposed method achieves 31.33% test mAP@0.50 using only 78 labeled training volumes, corresponding to a 1.53x improvement over supervised-only training.   </details>

- **[Planning in 8 Tokens: A Compact Discrete Tokenizer for Latent World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05438)**  `arXiv:2603.05438`  
  _Dongwon Kim, Gawon Seo, Jinsung Lee, Minsu Cho, Suha Kwak_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World models provide a powerful framework for simulating environment dynamics conditioned on actions or instructions, enabling downstream tasks such as action planning or policy learning. Recent approaches leverage world models as learned simulators, but its application to decision-time planning remains computationally prohibitive for real-time control. A key bottleneck lies in latent representations: conventional tokenizers encode each observation into hundreds of tokens, making planning both slow and resource-intensive. To address this, we propose CompACT, a discrete tokenizer that compresses each observation into as few as 8 tokens, drastically reducing computational cost while preserving essential information for planning.   </details>

- **[SGR3 Model: Scene Graph Retrieval-Reasoning Model in 3D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04614)**  `arXiv:2603.04614`

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  3D scene graphs provide a structured representation of object entities and their relationships, enabling high-level interpretation and reasoning for robots while remaining intuitively understandable to humans. Existing approaches for 3D scene graph generation typically combine scene reconstruction with graph neural networks (GNNs). However, such pipelines require multi-modal data that may not always be available, and their reliance on heuristic graph construction can constrain the prediction of relationship triplets. In this work, we introduce a Scene Graph Retrieval-Reasoning Model in 3D (SGR3 Model), a training-free framework that leverages multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for semantic scene graph generation. Moreover, an ablation study on the retrieval module and knowledge base scale reveals that retrieved external information is explicitly integrated into the token generation process, rather than being implicitly internalized through abstraction.
  </details>

- **[EraseAnything++: Enabling Concept Erasure in Rectified Flow Transformers Leveraging Multi-Object Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00978)**  `arXiv:2603.00978`  
  _Zhaoxin Fan, Nanxiang Jiang, Daiheng Gao, Shiji Zhou, Wenjun Wu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Removing undesired concepts from large-scale text-to-image (T2I) and text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models while preserving overall generative quality remains a major challenge, particularly as modern models such as Stable Diffusion v3, Flux, and OpenSora employ flow-matching and transformer-based architectures and extend to long-horizon video generation. Existing concept erasure methods, designed for earlier T2I/T2V models, often fail to generalize to these paradigms. To address this issue, we propose EraseAnything++, a unified framework for concept erasure in both image and video diffusion models with flow-matching objectives. Central to our approach is formulating concept erasure as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem that explicitly balances concept removal with preservation of generative utility. To solve the resulting conflicting objectives, we introduce an efficient utility-preserving unlearning strategy based on implicit gradient surgery. Furthermore, by integrating LoRA-based parameter tuning with attention-level regularization, our method anchors erasure on key visual representations and propagates it consistently across spatial and temporal dimensions. In the video setting, we further enhance consistency through an anchor-and-propagate mechanism that initializes erasure on reference frames and enforces it throughout subsequent transformer layers, thereby mitigating temporal drift. Extensive experiments on both image and video benchmarks demonstrate that EraseAnything++ substantially outperforms prior methods in erasure effectiveness, generative fidelity, and temporal consistency, establishing a new state of the art for concept erasure in next-generation diffusion models.
  </details>

- **[Effect of Patch Size on Fine-Tuning Vision Transformers in Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18614)**  `arXiv:2602.18614`  
  _Massoud Dehghan, Ramona Woitek, Amirreza Mahbod_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision Transformers (ViTs) and their variants have become state-of-the-art in many computer vision tasks. While substantial research has focused on architectural improvements, the impact of patch size, a crucial design choice in ViTs, remains underexplored, particularly in medical domains where both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) imaging modalities exist. In this study, using 12 medical imaging datasets from various imaging modalities (including seven 2D and five 3D datasets), we conduct a thorough evaluation of how different patch sizes affect ViT classification performance. Using a single graphical processing unit (GPU) and a range of patch sizes (1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28), we fine-tune ViT models and observe consistent improvements in classification performance with smaller patch sizes (1, 2, and 4), which achieve the best results across nearly all datasets. More specifically, our results indicate improvements in balanced accuracy of up to 12.78 percentage points for 2D datasets (patch size 2 vs. 28) and up to 23.78 percentage points for 3D datasets (patch size 1 vs. 14), at the cost of increased computational expense. Moreover, by combining the models trained with patch sizes 1, 2, and 4 using four fusion strategies, we achieve further performance gains in most cases, particularly for the 2D datasets. We further investigate the generalizability of these findings across higher image resolutions, different transformer architectures, and varying amounts of training data, observing performance trends similar to those of the main experiments. Our full implementation, along with guidelines for running the code, is publicly available on GitHub:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[StereoAdapter-2: Globally Structure-Consistent Underwater Stereo Depth Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16915)**  `arXiv:2602.16915`  
  _Zeyu Ren, Xiang Li, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Tang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Stereo depth estimation is fundamental to underwater robotic perception, yet suffers from severe domain shifts caused by wavelength-dependent light attenuation, scattering, and refraction. Recent approaches leverage monocular foundation models with GRU-based iterative refinement for underwater adaptation; however, the sequential gating and local convolutional kernels in GRUs necessitate multiple iterations for long-range disparity propagation, limiting performance in large-disparity and textureless underwater regions. Combined with dynamic LoRA adaptation inherited from StereoAdapter, our framework achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on underwater benchmarks with 17% improvement on TartanAir-UW and 7.2% improvment on SQUID, with real-world validation on the BlueROV2 platform demonstrates the robustness of our approach. Code:this https URL. Website:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[VLM-UQBench: A Benchmark for Modality-Specific and Cross-Modality Uncertainties in Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09214)**  `arXiv:2602.09214`  
  _Chenyu Wang, Tianle Chen, Yuxin Wu, Qijia He, Mingyu Chen, H. M. Sabbir Ahmad, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of vision-language models (VLMs). A central challenge is to identify the source of uncertainty, whether it arises from the image, the text, or their interaction.
