Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.
  </details>

- **[Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28158)**  `arXiv:2611.28158`  
  _Shardul Bansal, Seth Schilbe, Jarrod Barnes_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.
  </details>

- **[Lift Out, Kick In: Decoupling Event Effects for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27191)**  `arXiv:2611.27191`  
  _Yunying Zhu, Zichun Cao, Siwei Sun, Xiaocen Guo, Shengsheng Lin, Jing Hu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Real-world time series are often shaped by exogenous events whose effects are superimposed on the system's underlying temporal dynamics. Historical observations therefore entangle persistent dynamics with event-induced deviations, making it difficult to determine which patterns should be extrapolated and which should be attributed to specific event contexts. Existing event-aware forecasting methods can incorporate event information or model event-related variation, but typically treat historical event attribution and future event generation separately. We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), a general event-aware forecasting framework built on a shared Event Response Function (ERF). The ERF models event effects according to event type and relative temporal position and is shared across the historical and forecast windows. Loki lifts out estimated event-induced deviations from historical observations before forecasting, then uses the same ERF to kick in responses to known future events. This formulation separates event-response modeling from temporal forecasting while coupling historical attribution and future generation through a shared mechanism. Across five forecasting benchmarks, Loki achieves the best standardized MAE on all five datasets, reducing error by approximately 2.2%-11.7% over the strongest non-Loki baseline. Ablations and controlled analyses further support the roles of Lift Out, Kick In, shared response modeling, and compatibility across forecasting backbones.
  </details>

- **[Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25165)**  `arXiv:2611.25165`  
  _Anh Tien Nguyen, Dimitris Samaras, Mahdi S. Hosseini_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.
  </details>

- **[RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24395)**  `arXiv:2611.24395`  
  _Hanlin Wu, Yifei Wang, Zhicheng Cai, Wenxuan Tan, Jiahao Li, Huan-ang Gao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.
  </details>

- **[Find, Count and Fix Wrong Labels from a Trained Model, without Clean Labels or Shared Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22449)**  `arXiv:2611.22449`  
  _Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li, Nguyen H. Tran, Ken-Tye Yong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The question arises when labels are accepted from annotators and when a trained model is taken over with its training data. Readings from a model's outputs fail once it fits its wrong labels, because a fitted wrong label has a small loss and the prediction agrees with it. We read it from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. We normalise the magnitudes of an example's gradient into a gradient allocation, which records where the example asks the network to change, and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold, needs no clean data, held-out set or further training, and the data owner can compute the few numbers per example it needs, so the data need not be shared: a decoder trained to invert these numbers recovers images no closer to the originals than the mean image of their class. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where the loss, gradient norm and self-influence fall to 0.73-0.76. Over 22 image and 9 text settings it is the highest of the scores that read only the final model in every setting. On a fitted model it reads 54-96% of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10, where readings from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6%. Retraining without the flagged examples raises the test accuracy by up to 47 points, while removing as many random examples does not. Confident learning, given four further trainings on all the data, is not significantly better and flags less precisely. Auditing 5,000 images takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.
  </details>

- **[UrbanROI: Causal Modeling for Regional ROI Forecasting under POI Entry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20180)**  `arXiv:2611.20180`  
  _Zhaoqi Zhang, Miao Xie, Linyou Cai, Qianlong Xie, Xingxing Wang, Siqiang Luo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As urban commercial environments continue to evolve rapidly, accurately modeling the economic impact of point of interest (POI) entry is essential for supporting data-driven advertising allocation, merchant onboarding, and regional business decision-making. Existing return on investment (ROI) prediction methods mainly focus on individual ads or merchants, overlooking the interaction effects among POIs and failing to capture the causal influence of structural changes in urban commercial ecosystems. In this paper, we introduce a novel research problem -- regional ROI forecasting under POI entry, which aims to predict the future ROI trajectory of a commercial region after the introduction of a new POI by modeling temporal ROI evolution and competition-driven interactions among surrounding POIs. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal forecasting framework for region-level economic outcome prediction. UrbanROI leverages an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to explicitly model competitive relationships among POIs based on user request contexts, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets demonstrate that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in temporal economic modeling, inter-POI interaction representation, and intervention-aware forecasting, providing support for regional economic analysis in dynamic urban commercial systems. Source code is available at GitHub.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19634)**  `arXiv:2611.19634`  
  _Muhammad Qasim Elahi, Mahsa Ghasemi, Murat Kocaoglu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.
  </details>

- **[On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19207)**  `arXiv:2611.19207`  
  _Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Yi Yu, Gongli Xi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.
  </details>

- **[Asymmetric Multimodal Learning: The Alignment Redundancy Bound and Decomposed JEPAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16639)**  `arXiv:2611.16639`  
  _Yusuf Shihata_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cross-modal alignment is the default objective for multimodal representation learning, but it rests on an implicit assumption: that the two modalities are roughly symmetric views of the same underlying state. We show that this assumption fails on real multimodal data, and that alignment as a sole objective is provably lossy under informational asymmetry. We formalize the failure through Partial Information Decomposition, proving that cross-modal alignment retains at most the redundant information atom and annihilates the modality-unique and synergistic structure on which asymmetric tasks depend. We give the exact PID decomposition of the alignment information bottleneck, characterize its failure regime, and derive a sufficiency condition that any encoder objective must satisfy to preserve all four informational atoms. We then introduce Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA), which realizes this condition by factorizing each modality's latent space into an aligned shared core and a private fiber anchored by contextual masked prediction. On compositional reasoning benchmarks, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on relational queries; D-JEPA prevents this collapse, recovering the referent structure alignment discards, restoring most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and producing positive multimodal synergy where alignment inverts it. Information-theoretic and causal audits confirm that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.
  </details>

- **[Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control under Regime-Switching Demand: A Controlled Comparison of LSTM, MLP, and (s,S) Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15945)**  `arXiv:2611.15945`  
  _Alex Haines, Nathanael L. Baisa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Classical inventory policies such as (s,S) are provably optimal under stationary demand but cannot adapt when demand switches between hidden regimes, and memoryless deep reinforcement learning policies, confined to a fixed observation window, cannot maintain a belief over latent demand structure. We ask whether a recurrent policy offers a measurable advantage over both a memoryless policy and a classical baseline under regime-switching demand, and how that advantage scales with supply-chain lead time. We build a custom Gymnasium environment in which daily demand is generated by a two-state hidden Markov process with Poisson emissions, so that the regime is known at evaluation time but hidden from the agent. An optimised (s,S) heuristic, an MLP PPO agent, and an LSTM Recurrent PPO agent are trained under matched compute and evaluated at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each. The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time, and its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17$\times$ at lead time 10. Principal component analysis of the LSTM hidden state explains the widening gap: the representation shifts from encoding a binary regime indicator at short lead times to encoding multi-step pipeline state at long lead times. Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon lengthens.
  </details>

- **[From Shots to Rallies to Sets: Hierarchy-Aligned Multi-Task Learning for Next-Shot Prediction in Racket Sports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15529)**  `arXiv:2611.15529`  
  _Chao-Wei Cai, Min-Te Sun, Sheng Kuang Wu, Hung-Hsuan Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Next-shot prediction in racket sports requires learning from event data with different match structures, recorded attributes, and label vocabularies. Table tennis, badminton, and tennis nevertheless share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units. We present MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that uses this structure to jointly predict the attributes of the next shot. A hierarchical temporal Transformer captures event progression at each level of the hierarchy, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along the time axis, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets. Across four datasets from three sports, the final MT-HTA achieves the highest mean task-averaged F1 among the compared main models. Ablations on table tennis support the combination of hierarchical encoding, task attention, and feature-token interaction. Additional modules alter the balance between classification scores and spatial error rather than improving every metric. These results support a reusable architecture for heterogeneous racket-sport event data. We release the code for reproducibility.this https URL
  </details>

- **[Dual Representation Enhanced Diffusion Policy for Flexible Job Shop Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15246)**  `arXiv:2611.15246`  
  _Yunyi Zhao, Wei Zhang, Cheng Xiang, Vadakkepat Prahlad, Zuming Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) is a fundamental and challenging optimization problem in smart manufacturing. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches can learn effective scheduling policies through interaction with the environment, their performance often degrades as problem scale and processing-time uncertainty increase. In this paper, we propose DredRL, a dual representation enhanced diffusion-policy reinforcement learning scheduler. DredRL first constructs enhanced dual representations of operations and machines through self- and cross-attention mechanisms to capture both intra-entity and inter-entity dependencies. A diffusion model is further employed as the policy network, generating scheduling decisions through iterative denoising conditioned on the encoded state to enhance policy expressiveness and robustness. Extensive experiments on synthetic, public, large-scale, and stochastic FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that DredRL outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based schedulers across most configurations. Compared with SOTA learning-based methods, DredRL reduces makespan by up to 5.44% on synthetic instances. It also achieves the best learning-based performance on three of four public benchmarks and outperforms the stochasticity-aware algorithms on stochastic benchmarks. These results demonstrate that combining enhanced dual representations with diffusion-based policies provides an effective and robust approach for large scale scalable FJSP scheduling in complicated environment.
  </details>

- **[Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15062)**  `arXiv:2611.15062`  
  _Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can we faithfully approximate the output of a dense Transformer multilayer perceptron (MLP) by enumerating only a small set of probable channel configurations? Our primary objective is to characterize and control approximation error under a fixed mask budget. Probabilistic state space enumeration (PSSE) links the selected masks to the residual in the MLP output. For a partition into channel groups, probability weighting makes the expectation over all possible masks equal to the dense output. We derive the exact residual for any retained set by weighting each group's output by the fraction of its inclusion probability outside the set. The omitted probability mass multiplied by the largest masked-output norm therefore bounds the absolute error. To select masks, NORDER-II adapts ORDER-II from network reliability. Under independent group inclusions, it computes an ordering once per layer from frozen weights and finds the $B$ masks with greatest total probability mass without listing all possibilities. With 32 groups, the mean number of masks needed to capture 95% of the mass ranges from 1,020 to 4,725 across models, out of more than four billion possibilities. Across 168 MLP layers in six language models, this approximation yields lower mean relative error than both ordinary and bias-corrected uniform sampling in all 1,008 equal-count comparisons. Our secondary objective is to improve inference efficiency through pruning. We count the distinct channels covered by each layer's retained masks and use those counts to allocate a fixed projection budget offline. The pruned models achieve lower held-out perplexity than both top-$k$ baselines in all 36 settings at matched MLP projection FLOPs. Target projection savings of 10%, 20%, and 30% yield mean decoder MLP speedups of $1.11\times$, $1.23\times$, and $1.36\times$ over dense MLPs, respectively.
  </details>

- **[GenISys: Integrated Ship Systems Design Using Subsystem-Conditional Tabular Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11622)**  `arXiv:2611.11622`  
  _Noah J. Bagazinski, Faez Ahmed_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Ship design requires coordinating coupled subsystems to satisfy engineering constraints and balance competing performance and cost objectives. Generative artificial intelligence has supported component design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion, and operation. This paper presents GenISys, a framework for generating integrated systems, demonstrated through early-stage bulk-carrier design. Its dataset contains 217,999 proposed designs, including 16,247 that satisfy the formulated engineering constraints. The proposed simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (SCDDPM) generates subsystems together, allowing each subsystem model to respond to changes elsewhere during generation. Experiments compare this approach with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation across five independent training runs per architecture. In a study targeting lower cost per tonne of cargo transported, designs were generated for a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles. SCDDPM produced designs satisfying the formulated engineering constraints and meeting a common low-cost target in 55.70% of generation requests, compared with 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model. These correspond to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, respectively, while maintaining similar estimated transport costs. These results show how generative artificial intelligence can coordinate subsystems to generate feasible, high-performing integrated systems.
  </details>

- **[Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10543)**  `arXiv:2611.10543`  
  _Yunfu Deng, Josiah P. Hanna_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.
  </details>

- **[TripletAD: Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection in Embedding Space with Rare Anomalies and Scarce Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10352)**  `arXiv:2611.10352`  
  _Sumit Wadhwa, Souvik Nath_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As AI and agentic systems automate more processes with less human review, data is increasingly represented, and passed between systems, as embeddings produced by pre-trained models. Detecting rare deviations in these embeddings is becoming a critical guardrail, yet anomaly detection methods were largely developed for hand-built tabular features, where gradient-boosted trees remain the method of choice. We propose TripletAD, a weakly supervised detector for embedding spaces in which anomalies are rare. TripletAD learns a triplet-margin embedding in which every triplet contains an anomaly, so the few anomalies are reused across the entire training set instead of being diluted by it, and calibrates a linear scoring head with a partial cross-entropy on anomalies and a relative-contrast hinge that separates the mean scores of anomalous and normal samples. Across 28 embedding datasets spanning text, images, speech and industrial inspection, TripletAD is consistently among the best-performing methods, matching or exceeding established state-of-the-art weakly supervised detectors (DevNet, PReNet and DeepSAD), supervised contrastive learning and gradient-boosted trees, and it outperforms them when anomalies are rare. On naturally rare speech data it is 43% above the strongest baseline and more than twice the established detectors; at a 1% anomaly rate it has the highest mean AUCPR of seven methods, 20% above DevNet; and pooled over 74 rare-anomaly settings it has the best average rank, with statistically significant gains over every baseline. In a case study on AI-agent traces, it locates the failing step more often than all six baselines, with accuracy on par with or above that reported for frontier LLM judges, at 0.17 ms per step. The method needs no per-dataset tuning and is insensitive to its loss weights and training length.
  </details>

- **[Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04571)**  `arXiv:2611.04571`  
  _Andrea Cenzato, Lukas Karch, Andre Luckow, Yoran Pichon, Francesco Pasqua, Abouzar Ghasemi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets. The dataset is available for download atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[On the Convergence of Vanilla Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise and Index Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03201)**  `arXiv:2611.03201`  
  _Kanata Oowada, Hideaki Iiduka_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Understanding how stochastic gradient noise affects the convergence of Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) is an important problem in stochastic optimization, particularly when the noise exhibits heavy-tailed behavior. In this paper, we investigate the convergence of vanilla Adam in both the expected risk and the empirical risk minimization, focusing on the effects of heavy-tailed population noise and index-sampling noise. For the empirical risk minimization, we establish convergence guarantees under Hölder smoothness, showing that heavy-tailed population noise can affect the convergence bounds through dataset-dependent constants that may increase with the dataset size. For the expected risk minimization, we firstly establish both asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for vanilla Adam under Hölder smoothness and bounded $\mathfrak{p}$-th moment assumptions, allowing for infinite-variance stochastic gradient noise. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates in terms of the expected squared gradient norm and show that the convergence rates deteriorate as $\mathfrak{p}$ decreases. Numerical experiments further support these theoretical findings and provide empirical evidence for the relevance of the sufficient conditions underlying our convergence analysis.
  </details>

- **[Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40736)**  `arXiv:2610.40736`  
  _Oussama Chelly, Michael E. Houle, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Muhammad Rajabinasab, Arthur Zimek_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.
  </details>

- **[LatentWeave: Test-Time Latent Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39557)**  `arXiv:2610.39557`  
  _Fanci Meng, Kun Wang, Guibin Zhang, Xinlei Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Ming Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies.
  </details>

- **[Auditing Contextual Knowledge in Multimodal Inference: A Controlled Study with Alpha-TCM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38754)**  `arXiv:2610.38754`  
  _Yucheng Liu, Everett X. Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Knowledge-guided multimodal prediction requires measuring how supplied assumptions affect predictions. We present a controlled knowledge-auditing study using Alpha-TCM, with separately represented observations, supplied knowledge and reviewer decisions. Bayesian committee accounting makes the contextual prior replaceable while observation encoders remain fixed. Fully simulated studies use ten paired seeds and four training sizes to compare context representations and intervene on prior assumptions. A compact-head follow-up does not reproduce the original marginal-fusion improvement at 1,200 cases. A further study crosses head depth and training policy on fresh evaluation cohorts. All 16 point estimates in this study favor knowledge, but only one survives Holm correction: at 600 cases, the two-layer extended-policy model reduces MAE by 0.00306 (1.33%) relative to learned-category conditioning. Extended training improves several methods' absolute performance, while relative advantages remain conditional. Wrong priors increase error in every seed across all tested depths, policies and sizes. Separately calibrated conflict thresholds flag 11.3-12.6% of wrong-prior cases in the compact-head follow-up but provide little guidance about individual prediction damage. The study provides a reproducible way to test supplied knowledge and distinguish predictive gains from sensitivity to misspecified assumptions.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Token Prediction Done Right](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38331)**  `arXiv:2610.38331`  
  _Jayden Teoh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Variational Optimal Control for Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37146)**  `arXiv:2610.37146`  
  _Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sampling-time guidance and reward-based post-training act on different variables but share a core geometric objective: realizing an output-space improvement through a generative model. We organize both around a Jacobian pullback evaluated with respect to either the current noisy state or the trainable parameters. Formulating current-state conditional variational optimal control (VOC) yields Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG), which transports a terminal reward proxy into a covariance-weighted sampling correction. Under a linear-subspace denoising model, the exact pullback has no component normal to the data subspace. Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) realizes the parameter-space counterpart of this local control principle: projected reward ascent constructs a bounded endpoint displacement within a local trust region, and a sparse, forward-pinned Euler surrogate transports it to LoRA parameters. Empirically, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID on ImageNet from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model and leads all trained comparators on these five means, while CLIP remains close to the base and DeQA declines across all trained methods. The shared pullback interface cleanly separates the desired output change from the model derivative and the actuation variable.
  </details>

- **[Advancement or Acceleration? How Data Curation Improves LLM Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36983)**  `arXiv:2610.36983`  
  _Jiaxing Wang, Zicheng Zhang, Deping Xiang, Jin Xu, Yong Li, Chao Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While data curation is widely credited with improving large language model training, a basic question remains unresolved: does curation expand what a model can ultimately learn, or reach the same solution faster? In this paper, we formalize this distinction between advancement (improving the attainable performance) and acceleration (reaching the same performance with less data). Through an analytic characterization and real-world LLM experiments, we show that advancement requires a correctable train-target gap. When the baseline training and target objectives coincide, no curation policy improves the endpoint, and its benefit is acceleration. This reframes advancement as a property of the curation task rather than the curation method. Under a common gap-centric view of data mixture and selection, we operationalize this condition as the $\Delta$-diagnostic, an observable discrepancy between the uncurated baseline's training and target losses that is computable prior to expensive curation. Across extensive experiments, an appreciably nonzero $\Delta$ predicts persistent gains, whereas gains near $\Delta=0$ tend to diminish as the training budget grows. Beyond individual methods, our findings recenter data curation on the task itself and point to target-set construction as a promising direction for shaping what curation can achieve.
  </details>

- **[CaPS: A causal world model for out-of-distribution physical parameter shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29088)**  `arXiv:2610.29088`  
  _Chu Lin, Yi Sun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A world model that serves as a robot's digital twin has to keep working when the robot changes, for example when its links become heavier than anything seen in training. We study this case on the TriFinger robot in CausalWorld, assuming that the link masses and the low-level control law are known. Our model, CaPS (a causal world model for physical parameter shifts), gives each finger a learned energy in which every movable link contributes a term scaled by its measured mass, plus one term that does not depend on mass. Inertia and bias forces both come from this energy, actions pass through the known proportional-derivative controller, and a residual network that never sees the masses accounts for contact. Trained with light links, CaPS forecasts 100 steps open loop on three disjoint test ranges whose mean masses are 1.86, 2.75, and 3.75 times the training mean, with median joint R2 of 0.773, 0.779, and 0.750; an ensemble-residual variant, CaPS-Ens, reaches 0.801, 0.784, and 0.753. Compared with separately trained controls that see only the training-mean mass, the true masses improve both models in all ten runs at every shift. A rigid-body calculation traces the mass-independent term to the fingertips, whose mass is not intervened on, and adding the same term to ModLaNet improves it at every shift.
  </details>

- **[CIS-Transolver: A neural operator for fine-scale automotive aerodynamic flow prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26337)**  `arXiv:2610.26337`  
  _Jianglong Liu, Zhicheng Zhu, Jia Hao, Liangyue Jia, Wenxuan He_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automotive aerodynamic optimization requires accurate predictions of both vehicle-scale pressure and velocity distributions and local fine-scale spatial variations near complex geometries. Spectral bias in neural operators hinders the fitting of high-frequency spatial components, limiting fine-scale flow prediction. To mitigate this bias, we propose CIS-Transolver, an automotive flow prediction method that combines spatial representations of local multiscale variations with cross-layer state updates. Geometric moments of orders zero through two encode local feature increments and their spatial correlations, while current observations are combined with states retained from preceding layers to form cross-layer memory. This memory is fed back through the value branch of Physics-Attention at each layer, allowing local fine-scale variations to continually inform the prediction of the overall flow field. CIS-Transolver is evaluated on three public automotive flow datasets, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, for predicting vehicle surface pressure and surrounding three-dimensional pressure and velocity fields. Across all five prediction tasks, it achieves the lowest mean relative L2 errors and corresponding high-frequency spectral errors among the methods compared. Relative to the best-performing baseline for each task and metric, the relative reductions, averaged across the five tasks, are 8.72% and 16.06%, respectively. Spatial increment analysis further demonstrates improved prediction of local pressure and velocity variations. These improvements in overall flow accuracy and high-frequency prediction provide more accurate flow information for automotive aerodynamic performance assessment and design optimization.
  </details>

- **[Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18001)**  `arXiv:2610.18001`  
  _Miao Li, Hanyang Jiang, Hengyu Fu, Baihe Huang, Yating Liu, Yuhang Cai, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
  </details>

- **[LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics Toward Long-Horizon Rollouts in World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15267)**  `arXiv:2610.15267`  
  _Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. We measure rollout collapse on the data, with four ratios of the rollout to the truth, on five environments learned from pixels: conservative and actuated pendulums, a mass-spring, a two-body system and a cart pole. With the encoder and latent state held fixed, an MLP and a transformer predictor contract the rollout on every environment, while LeHami's rollouts do not merge. LeHami is the most accurate of the three at long horizons, in position on four of the five environments and in velocity on three, while at short horizons the free predictors are more accurate on two of the five. The learned flow also integrates at unseen sub-frame step sizes and, run backward with the recorded actions, recovers earlier frames as well as it predicts later ones. LeWM, with a richer three-frame encoder of its own, is more accurate on four of the five, which suggests incorporating a richer encoder within LeHami in future work. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
  </details>

- **[When Generative Models Act as Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12847)**  `arXiv:2610.12847`  
  _Sevan Brodjian, Michael Hobley, Pietro Perona_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model acts as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. We test two kinds of state mappings, both fit from latent states paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the simulator-to-latent mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even when steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, in ways decodability does not predict. In Othello, each simplification of the rules lowers editability. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. Editability across layers suggests that the Othello model compresses its history into a board partway through the network, while the Rayworld model shifts its recent frames and then refines a rendering of the next frame. The inverse map succeeds by approximating this partial rendering. We relate both outcomes to the causal state of computational mechanics, the minimal summary of its history a model must keep to predict optimally, which may not align with the simulator. Guided by this view, we change how the Rayworld model is trained and make its state more simulator-like.
  </details>

- **[Ambient Discrete Diffusion: Using the Wrong Data at the Right Time for Data Efficient Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12340)**  `arXiv:2610.12340`  
  _Julian Kleutgens, Mauricio Tec, Claudio Battiloro, Francesca Dominici, Giannis Daras_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce RefineMix, a framework for training discrete diffusion models under severe data scarcity, a common constraint in scientific applications. RefineMix uses out-of-distribution data at selected diffusion times to improve generalization without biasing the sampling distribution. Although this strategy has been explored in continuous diffusion, discrete diffusion presents a distinct challenge: unlike Gaussian noise, masking preserves domain information in surviving tokens, limiting the use of related data at high noise levels. At low noise levels, however, the domains effectively disjoint supports become an advantage, allowing the model to learn from both in-domain and out-of-distribution data without biasing the sampler. We formalize these intuitions and provide a theoretical analysis for the proposed method. Experimentally, across five domain-shift settings, RefineMix matches or outperforms in-domain finetuning and data mixing. For protein sequence generation, finetuning with just 197 in-domain examples nearly doubles the fraction of generated proteins that are simultaneously novel, foldable, and in-family compared to standard finetuning.
  </details>

- **[Fully Interpretable Minimal Transformers: From Geometry to Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09838)**  `arXiv:2610.09838`  
  _Raneem Mahajne, Toviah Moldwin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present a framework for building and interpreting minimal transformer models. By constraining a transformer's embedding dimension and head size to 2, we enable full two-dimensional visualization of its internal representations. Embeddings, query/key/value transforms, attention outputs, residual streams, and decision boundaries can all be seen directly. Our central claim is that the learned geometry implies an algorithm. The arrangement of points and boundaries in R^2 can be read as a step-by-step procedure. We train a transformer on a simple task where it must produce the most recently observed even number whenever the '+' operator appears in a sequence of digits. Once trained, we visually walk through every step of the transformer's computation. We show how the model embeds the tokens and their respective positions in the sequence, transforms them via the Q, K, and V matrices, uses the dot product between the Q and K representations to form the attention matrix, and uses the attention matrix to select values that move the representation of each input token embedding to the region of the domain of the output layer that will correctly predict the next token. We introduce a suite of interpretability visualizations that make the algorithmic interpretation of this procedure explicit. Our framework offers a pedagogical and experimental testbed to explore how transformers use information geometry to implement next-token prediction.
  </details>

- **[Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09221)**  `arXiv:2610.09221`  
  _Yuxiang Fu, Qi Yan, Zike Wu, Yongxing Zhang, Purang Abolmaesumi, Lele Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, orchestration of multiple objectives, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity of the teacher model. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network, which greatly simplifies the distribution matching distillation pipeline. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. On text-to-image distillation tasks, our method also enable fast high-fidelity generation with no image data required. Our code code and model are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[LeAVJEPA: A Minimalist Architecture for Audio-Visual Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06226)**  `arXiv:2610.06226`  
  _Benjamin Robson, Santeri Mentu, Wenshuai Zhao, Arno Solin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Prior audio-visual self-supervised learning methods rely on mechanisms such as EMA target encoders, prediction heads, reconstruction decoders, and contrastive losses. We introduce LeAVJEPA, the first audio-visual encoder trained under LeJEPA's collapse-free objective. A single early-fusion Vision Transformer processes audio, video, and joint audio-video inputs. Modality dropout treats a missing modality as another view of the same event, making cross-modal alignment implicit in the objective. The model aligns global embeddings with modality-specific local embeddings, and SIGReg prevents representational collapse. A controlled ablation identifies modality dropout as the key mechanism for audio-visual alignment. Despite the architectural simplicity, LeAVJEPA reaches 36.0 mAP on AudioSet-20K and 91.3% accuracy on ESC-50 under frozen evaluation. After fine-tuning, it reaches 61.1% accuracy on VGGSound, and its embeddings support zero-shot audio-visual retrieval.
  </details>

- **[Direction-Conditioned Policies for Online Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05087)**  `arXiv:2610.05087`  
  _S K Swaminathan, Damiya Gondha, Theyanesh Eswaramoorthy Rajahkrishnan, Aritra Hazra_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) learns representations that estimate goal reachability, yet its policy remains conditioned on raw goals and therefore does not directly exploit the geometry encoded by its critic. We introduce Direction-Conditioned Policies (DCP), a method built around a small modification to CRL: DCP selects previously visited states as waypoints during online training and conditions the policy on their direction and distance in representation space. At deployment, DCP applies the same interface directly to the final goal, requiring neither waypoint selection nor planning. Across nine navigation and manipulation tasks, DCP attains higher final success rates than CRL on seven tasks and spends more time near the goal on seven. Ablations show that most of the gains come from conditioning on direction and distance, while the waypoints let DCP learn on every task, including those where the goal is rarely reached early in training. Controlled maze experiments further show that DCP captures shortest-path geometry more accurately and that the supplied direction causally influences the actor's behavior. Finally, we show that learned candidate generation improves goal reaching in two controlled mazes.
  </details>

- **[Latent Information Sharing for Accelerating Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01126)**  `arXiv:2610.01126`  
  _Seungjun Lee, Ensieh Khazaei, Dimitrios Hatzinakos, Baturalp Buyukates, Sunwoo Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Federated learning (FL) is a communication-efficient distributed learning paradigm. However, client drift remains one of the most critical challenges, hindering the efficient training of a global model. In this study, we propose a novel latent information sharing scheme that directly mitigates data heterogeneity across clients. Our theoretical and empirical results show that sharing a small amount of hidden-layer activations significantly improves training efficiency while preserving convergence guarantees and data privacy. Furthermore, we compare our method with existing FL approaches designed to address client drift, including FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedPVR, FedProto, and SplitFed, and demonstrate superior model accuracy under a fixed round budget without incurring excessive communication overhead. Overall, this work presents a promising new knowledge aggregation scheme and provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of activation sharing on federated optimization.
  </details>

- **[Disentangling Lung-Cancer CT/LDCT AI: A Systematic Evidence Map of Clinical Tasks, Evidence Chains, and Translational Gaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35240)**  `arXiv:2609.35240`  
  _Surajit Das_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  \textbf{Background:} Artificial-intelligence studies using computed tomography (CT) for lung cancer are often broadly labelled ``prediction'' despite addressing clinically distinct tasks.\textbf{Methods:} We systematically mapped CT/low-dose CT (LDCT)-centered lung-cancer AI using five-database retrieval, full-text eligibility assessment, role-aware modality/omics extraction, clinical-task classification, and a Multi-Tier Evidence Graph (MTEG).\textbf{Results:} The final corpus comprised 278 studies (2016--2026): 216 Detection, 7 future Risk-prediction, and 55 Other studies. Clinical variables (96.0\%), 3-D CT/LDCT (74.5\%), and radiomics (64.0\%) predominated, whereas external validation (28.4\%), calibration (20.1\%), decision-curve analysis (13.3\%), longitudinal CT (17.3\%), and saliency/attribution XAI (21.6\%) were less frequent. The fixed-extraction MTEG comprised 359 nodes and 3,284 edges. Of 278 studies, 31 (11.15\%) covered all six substantive tiers, with the greatest attrition at reasoning/explanation. With explanation optional, 110 studies (39.6\%) covered the remaining five tiers.\textbf{Conclusions:} Overall, the literature is detection-dominated, genuine future risk prediction remains uncommon, and complete translational evidence chains are rare in the extracted map. Limited omics-role recall constrains interpretation of the mapped molecular-input frequencies.
  </details>

- **[Muon Sublates the Edge of Stability in LLM Pretraining: What Persists and What Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34915)**  `arXiv:2609.34915`  
  _Yanzhe Chen, Qifang Zhao, Xiaoxiao Xu, Fanghui Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Muon is increasingly used for language-model pretraining, yet its large-step dynamics are not captured by the classical edge-of-stability (EoS) picture of gradient descent (GD). We study stochastic (no-momentum) Muon through theoretical analysis, controlled networks, and language models from 22M to 1B parameters, distinguishing three diagnostics: generalized sharpness, loss balance, and update alignment. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that loss balance differs from its generalized sharpness and cannot determine update alignment across various learning rates in 130M pre-training as well as 1B runs. Besides, our experiments also show that increasing the batch size encourages update alignment towards to total reversal. Furthermore, checkpoint interventions in the 22M and 130M models show that increasing the learning rate can initially raise the loss but a lower validation loss at the end of the prescribed warmup-stable-decay continuation. These results support a split EoS picture: generalized-sharpness saturation persists in the measured runs, but loss balance and update geometry require separate characterization, allowing for learning-rate schedules design. The source code for reproducing the experiments can be found inthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Loop Dropout: Regularizing Shared Updates in Looped Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34218)**  `arXiv:2609.34218`  
  _Zirui Zhu, Hailun Xu, Xuanlei Zhao, Yong Liu, Yingxuan Ren, Kanchan Sarkar, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Looped language models separate computational depth from parameter count by repeatedly applying the same transformer block. Adapting these models requires a shared update that remains effective as hidden states evolve throughout the recurrent computation. Our empirical analysis reveals a pronounced late-loop bias in standard low-rank adaptation (LoRA): the shared update provides limited adaptation at early loop positions. This imbalance motivates training shared updates under varying combinations of their applications. Randomly omitting adapter applications alone, however, does not improve task performance; it reduces expected update strength during training while leaving inference unchanged. We introduce Loop Dropout, which couples stochastic masking of adapter applications with inverse-survival rescaling to preserve expected update strength and promote effective adaptation across loops. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved mathematical reasoning across model sizes, adapter ranks and training recipes, with benefits extending to general instruction tuning and code generation. Loop Dropout outperforms existing LoRA variants and adapter regularizers, while further analysis shows stronger early-loop adaptation. Every backbone loop remains active, and inference applies the adapter at all loops using standard LoRA without additional trainable parameters or inference computation. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Surprising Success, Repeated Failure: Entropy-Guided Credit Assignment for Exploration in LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33781)**  `arXiv:2609.33781`  
  _Woongyeong Yeo, Minki Kang, Chanuk Lee, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through outcome-level feedback, yet recent approaches to finer-grained credit assignment often require auxiliary models, additional sampling, or privileged information. Although policy entropy provides a readily available signal, prioritizing uncertain positions under both reinforcement and penalization concentrates penalties where failed responses still retain alternatives for recovery, which can suppress opportunities for exploration. To address this, we introduce Entropic Advantage Policy Optimization (EAPO), an entropy-guided credit assignment method that treats success and failure asymmetrically. Specifically, motivated by the observation that success under uncertainty is less repeatable while confident failures tend to recur, EAPO couples normalized policy entropy with the sign of the response advantage to reinforce surprising success and correct repeated failure. It assigns stronger reinforcement to high-entropy decisions in successful responses and stronger penalties to low-entropy decisions in failed responses, while attenuating penalties at uncertain positions to preserve opportunities for recovery. By redistributing the response advantage across tokens, EAPO derives token-level credit directly from existing rollout signals without additional supervision. We validate EAPO on a range of reasoning tasks across both base and reasoning backbones, demonstrating that it achieves the best overall performance. We further show that EAPO promotes more effective exploration, broadening problem coverage and diversifying successful reasoning strategies.
  </details>

- **[ALDER: Discovering the Laws of a World by Acting in It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33728)**  `arXiv:2609.33728`  
  _Teng Cao, Yu Deng, Quentin Delfosse, Kristian Kersting_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reliable world models should not only predict future states but express how actions change the world in an explicit, transparent and testable form, such as equations. Yet methods that rely on a fixed set of trajectories cannot distinguish equally good competing hypotheses, while searches over a fixed set of predefined candidates cannot discover equations outside the initial hypothesis space. We introduce ALDER (Action-guided Law Discovery, Evaluation, and Revision), a method that actively proposes novel experiments to test and revise models. Specifically, ALDER proposes parametric equations; a numerical optimizer fits their coefficients; an independent verifier tests these candidates on held-out data. To distinguish between competing valid hypotheses, a cost- and safety-aware selector queries interventions, in the form of novel experiments. The resulting counterexamples update the evidence ledger and guide the next structural revision, while incompatible laws are discarded. Across an in-house benchmark, ODE equation discovery tasks, and robotic experiments, ALDER discovers laws beyond its initial formula set, repairs failed model proposals, distinguishes fixed candidate models with fewer interactions, and improves out-of-distribution prediction. Furthermore, given a current state and a target, ALDER selects control actions by solving the inverse problem defined by its validated world model. Together, these results show that explicit equation-based world models can be tested and revised through interaction, then naturally used to guide goal-directed control.
  </details>

- **[Can Circuit Alignment Predict OOD Generalization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31996)**  `arXiv:2609.31996`  
  _Ayan Banerjee, Abhra Chaudhuri, Josep Llados, Umapada Pal, Anjan Dutta_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization be predicted from a trained model's weights alone, without any target-domain data? Existing representational similarity metrics (CKA, SVCCA, RSA) compare activations rather than forecast generalization. We show they are provably insensitive to structural rerouting in the computational graph, the very change distribution shift induces. We close this gap with the Circuit Alignment Score (CAS), which compares class-specific circuits across domains via graph kernels, decomposed into same-class coherence and cross-class confusion. Casting CAS as a Lebesgue integral over the domain distribution, we prove its Monte Carlo estimate recovers the ground-truth ranking of learners by OOD accuracy, with pairwise inversion error vanishing at rate $O(1/M)$, where $M$ is the number of sampled domains. Across $48$ learners on PACS, CAS attains $0.88$ rank correlation with OOD accuracy, versus $0.58$ (CKA), $0.23$ (SVCCA), and $0.14$ (RSA), with similar trends on other benchmarks and even against data-dependent methods, making it the first provably consistent predictor of distributional robustness requiring neither target-domain data nor labels. The code is available at:this https URL
  </details>

- **[The Sequential Price of Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29674)**  `arXiv:2609.29674`  
  _Zonghuan Xu, Xingjun Ma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sequential task updates are fundamental to continual learning, but their recency bias can impose a lasting performance cost. We study this cost in an overparameterized linear-regression model with i.i.d. task sampling. We prove that distribution-level forgetting and population loss converge to the same stationary limit. We quantify the additional loss incurred by sequential exact fitting, or the sequential price. If all nonzero eigenvalues of all task curvature matrices equal the same constant, the stationary loss is exactly twice the joint-training optimum. We further analyze fixed-strength elastic weight consolidation (EWC) under general task curvatures and characterize its stationary sequential price at every regularization strength. Under strong regularization, the price decays inversely with EWC strength while the number of tasks sufficient to reduce the mean-square effect of initialization by a fixed factor grows proportionally. Real Jester user ratings, with a natural encoding and training procedure, satisfy our theoretical assumptions.
  </details>

- **[Interweaving Marginals into Multivariate Sample Paths: Training-Free Dependence Construction for Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25980)**  `arXiv:2609.25980`  
  _Jinmyeong Choi, Jinkwan Jang, Seul Lee, Taesup Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Probabilistic time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide coordinate-wise predictive distributions, but these marginals do not determine a joint distribution over multivariate future trajectories. We study training-free coupling of frozen TSFM marginals into multivariate forecast sample paths. Our primary evaluation fixes the empirical marginal sample multiset at every channel--horizon coordinate across methods, isolating the effect of coupling alone. Historical temporal and channel relations substantially improve their corresponding dependence diagnostics. The same pattern persists when the fixed-marginal constraint is removed and paths are sampled directly, and remains present under native multivariate backbone inference. These results support treating dependence reconstruction as a distinct post-processing problem for probabilistic TSFMs.
  </details>

- **[SAVOR: Score Once, Learn Deeper in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24141)**  `arXiv:2609.24141`  
  _Keye Zheng, Hanyu Li, Zhan Cheng, Yuan Gao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own samples with token-level scores from a stronger teacher, and it effectively transfers reasoning ability to small language models. We observe that reusing the batch alone is not enough, because no single fixed teacher target suits every batch. In our runs, a fixed $\alpha$ of 0.3 exceeds a KL envelope at every training step, while 0.2 leaves over a quarter of it unused. We propose SAVOR, which selects for each batch the strongest teacher target inside the KL envelope, freezes the scored batch, and reuses it for a fixed number of student updates without further teacher calls. On five math reasoning benchmarks with a 1.7B student and a 30B-A3B teacher, SAVOR raises macro accuracy over TOP-D from 15.41 to 17.78 with two passes and to 19.36 with three passes at about the same teacher budget. With three passes, SAVOR nearly matches the final accuracy of TOP-D after one third of training while using 67.2% fewer teacher-scored tokens. These results suggest budgeting reuse depth explicitly in OPD.
  </details>

- **[Preserving Geometric Integrity in Graph Prompting via Measure-Constrained Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23547)**  `arXiv:2609.23547`  
  _Xiangyu Wang, Shuo Wang, Ruiyi Fang, Zhao Kang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Graph prompt learning enables parameter-efficient adaptation of frozen Graph Neural Networks to downstream tasks through lightweight prompt parameters. As routing becomes increasingly node-adaptive, however, independently optimized local decisions can collectively concentrate assignment mass on a small subset of a finite shared prompt bank, even when individual node--prompt matches remain locally meaningful. We propose MINT (Measure-INtegrity Transport), an entropically regularized optimal transport framework that formulates node-to-prompt adaptation as a globally coupled allocation problem. The transport cost favors local geometric compatibility, while a prescribed prompt-side marginal explicitly controls graph-wide prompt utilization. We further derive an exact variance decomposition that separates prompt-side geometric variance into retained prompt-update variation and within-node barycentric dispersion, together with a conditional stability bound for the frozen-encoder forward map. Across standard citation networks and additional heterophilic graphs, MINT remains competitive in few-shot adaptation. Controlled and end-to-end experiments further distinguish the roles of routing and topology: fixed-marginal routing controls graph-wide prompt utilization and has measurable end-to-end effects on citation networks, while topology augmentation provides a complementary, graph-dependent mechanism for addressing structural mismatch. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[On the Recall Scaling Laws in Mamba: A Theoretical and Mechanistic Study via Hashing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07681)**  `arXiv:2609.07681`  
  _Yuval Koren, Assaf Ben-Kish, Raja Giryes, Lior Wolf, Itamar Zimerman_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Associative Recall (AR) is the cognitive ability to learn and retrieve links between items in memory. In NLP, AR is used as a benchmark for evaluating the in-context memory capacity of architectures such as Mamba, and has been found to strongly correlate with language modeling performance. This paper explores AR from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability, aiming to reverse-engineer the exact internal algorithm used by Mamba to perform recall. Our key insight is that Mamba performs recall by implicitly learning linear hash functions, and we identify the low-level circuit that enables this behavior. Building on these findings and inspired by theoretical tools in similarity-preserving hashing, such as the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing AR, which we term Recall Scaling Laws. Given the vocabulary size and the number of facts in context, this framework allows us to (1) predict the embedding and state dimensions required for Mamba to achieve perfect recall, (2) predict recall success probability given the model dimensions, and (3) analyze multi-layer models and multi-head SSM patterns. Empirical results show that our theoretical findings are accurate and predictive, offering insights into how AR capacity scales with vocabulary, state, embedding size, and architecture.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21308)**  `arXiv:2608.21308`  
  _Zeyun Zhong, Joya Chen, Manuel Martin, Frederik Diederichs, Juergen Gall, Juergen Beyerer_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
