- **[Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28387)**  `arXiv:2611.28387`  
  _Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.
  </details>

- **[Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28346)**  `arXiv:2611.28346`  
  _Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.
  </details>

- **[Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28319)**  `arXiv:2611.28319`  
  _Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
  </details>

- **[Probing Invisible Actuation Shifts for Test-time Calibration of Visuomotor Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28308)**  `arXiv:2611.28308`  
  _Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
  </details>

- **[FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28256)**  `arXiv:2611.28256`  
  _Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
  </details>

- **[5G NR Sensing of Robotic Arm Motion in Indoor Factory Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28053)**  `arXiv:2611.28053`  
  _Neeraj Varshney, Anuraag Bodi, Steve Blandino, Jian Wang, Camillo Gentile, Nada Golmie_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper investigates the performance of monostatic Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems for tracking robotic arm kinematics in industrial factory (InF) environments. Building on a part-specific quasi-deterministic channel model previously derived from high-resolution robotic-arm measurements using our context-aware channel sounder and digital twin, we develop a framework for generating arbitrary articulated motion profiles through hierarchical kinematic transformations. By integrating this high-fidelity target model with the standardized 3GPP InF channel model, we employ 5G New Radio (NR) Positioning Reference Signals (PRS) as the sensing waveform to enable comprehensive system-level evaluation. Simulations are conducted for both sparse clutters (InF-SH) and dense clutters (InF-DH) scenarios using 3GPP-compliant antenna radiation patterns and analog beamforming, allowing us to assess the impact of industrial clutter on sensing performance. The results show that while high estimation accuracy is achievable under Line-of-Sight (LOS) conditions, dense clutter in InF-DH environments introduces severe blockage that significantly limits sensing reliability. In particular, the effective sensing coverage in InF-DH is drastically reduced, with detection probability dropping to approximately \(P_d \approx 10\,\%\) even when the robotic arm is located directly beneath the Transmission Reception Point (TRP). Furthermore, in InF-SH, achieving a high detection probability (e.g., \(P_d \geq 90\,\%\)) requires the target to remain in close proximity to the TRP, with an effective coverage radius of approximately 13 m.
  </details>

- **[Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27689)**  `arXiv:2611.27689`  
  _Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
  </details>

- **[Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27182)**  `arXiv:2611.27182`  
  _Sunli Chen, Yun Zong, Qinhong Zhou, Xiaowen Qiu, Jiaben Chen, Zeyuan Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.
  </details>

- **[BeyondEgo: Learning to Act Beyond Egocentric Perception via Humanoid Ego-Exo Foresight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27047)**  `arXiv:2611.27047`  
  _Zhaoshan Yang, Chenglei Li, Haoyu Lei, Yutao Zhang, Yuyu Yang, Zhuo Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating whole-body motion to perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Yet egocentric vision-language-action (VLA) policies can miss critical body--scene relationships, and action imitation alone provides no explicit supervision for future scene evolution. We propose BeyondEgo to extend VLA perception in space and time. Spatially, we encode a synchronized exocentric view with frozen DINOv3 and concatenate the resulting tokens with egocentric VLM tokens to condition the action expert. Temporally, we use future observations from both views as privileged supervision for a residual adapter on task-conditioned VLM features. A foresight expert regresses DINOv3 representations of both views 0.6s ahead. At deployment, the foresight expert is discarded and the 4.2M-parameter adapter is retained. We also introduce HELM, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark with synchronized egocentric and exocentric views across five whole-body tasks. On HELM, BeyondEgo improves success from 48.0% to 92.0% in distribution and from 23.5% to 65.0% on 200 held-out scenes with layout, asset, material, and lighting shifts. Ablations show that dual-view DINOv3 foresight yields the best transfer results.
  </details>

- **[RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27042)**  `arXiv:2611.27042`  
  _Chenghao Yin, Da Huang, Di Yang, Jichao Wang, Junhui Wu, Nanshu Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
  </details>

- **[TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26405)**  `arXiv:2611.26405`  
  _Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
  </details>

- **[Learning optimal gaits and styles for terrain-adaptive quadruped locomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25958)**  `arXiv:2611.25958`  
  _Guillaume Bellegarda, Auke Ijspeert_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Animals use many different gaits to locomote at different speeds across varying terrains. A longstanding question in biology and robotics is: which gait is best? This question is most often addressed from an energy-efficiency perspective on flat terrain, leaving open how the answer depends on terrain and on the criterion optimized. Here we show that gait optimality is determined jointly by terrain, performance metric, and velocity. We use deep reinforcement learning and networks of abstract oscillators, modeling spinal central pattern generators, to learn 11 quadrupedal gaits across diverse challenging terrains, together with the locomotion style (base height, foot ground clearance, foot offsets) that each requires. A second policy then selects among them to optimize a user-specified criterion such as cost of transport, base stability, or joint smoothness. Across these performance metrics and within this repertoire, every gait is optimal under at least one terrain-metric-velocity combination. The framework adapts zero-shot to gait couplings and styles never seen during training, to terrains far beyond the training distribution, and to larger quadrupeds five times the training mass. With a single additional pitch-tracking reward term, the same gait couplings also support bipedal-mode locomotion. Our method provides a general and systematic way to produce expressive locomotion and to select the gait best suited to a given terrain and criterion. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25927)**  `arXiv:2611.25927`  
  _Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian, Haishan Liu, Changti Wu, Yu Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our project page is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[TipDex-VTLA: Learning to Refine Actions with Visual Reliability and Tactile Feedback for Dexterous Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25683)**  `arXiv:2611.25683`  
  _Xudi Ge, Yepeng Liu, Haifeng Liu, Enze Shi, Liangqi Zhang, Yongchao Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
  </details>

- **[RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23731)**  `arXiv:2611.23731`  
  _Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
  </details>

- **[JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22543)**  `arXiv:2611.22543`  
  _Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
  </details>

- **[ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21258)**  `arXiv:2611.21258`  
  _Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk is identical for every proposal and thus carries no proposal-specific signal, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
  </details>

- **[ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21115)**  `arXiv:2611.21115`  
  _Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes. Project Page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16645)**  `arXiv:2611.16645`  
  _Shaobo Yang, Zichen Ai, Ziyang Ma, Qian Yang, Bin Fang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
  </details>

- **[STVLA: Spatial-aware and Temporal-memory forVision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16589)**  `arXiv:2611.16589`  
  _Zhuo Han, Yeqiang Wang, Xinran Wang, Hongwei Han, Yi Xiong, Zunian Wan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{this https URL}{this https URL}
  </details>

- **[What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16246)**  `arXiv:2611.16246`  
  _Jinze Tao, Yuxiao Han, Kangkang Dong, Yancong Wei, Xiaojun Zhu, Bokui Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a task-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing a method trained on 10M samples.   _Jibao Yuan, Zixiang Zhao, Wensong Xu, Siqi Lu, Shaofei Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper focuses on improving the precision and adaptability of language-conditioned manipulation policies learned through imitation learning. Recently, action-based methods have become mainstream for closed-loop control, yet implicit behavior learning from demonstrations limits their generalization beyond training conditions. To address this, explicit geometric priors offer direct guidance for action prediction. In particular, 6-DoF grasp detection generates diverse grasp hypotheses with explicit approach directions for the gripper. Yet raw hypotheses span multiple regions and lack task semantics, requiring joint reasoning with the scene and instruction. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as explicit geometric priors. Specifically, it encodes multi-view point clouds, the instruction, and grasp hypotheses, binds task-relevant ones to scene context and task semantics via bidirectional cross-attention, and decodes continuous action chunks. Experiments show that, with 0.29B parameters, 39.5 ms latency, and no robot-data pretraining, GraSLA outperforms existing baselines, achieving 99.3% on LIBERO, 73.7% on LIBERO+, and 53.33% on LIBERO-Pro.
  </details>

- **[RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08209)**  `arXiv:2611.08209`  
  _Satvik Sharma, Hengyuan Hu, Mihika Kamat, Samrat Sahoo, Dorsa Sadigh, Jeannette Bohg_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available atthis http URL.
  </details>

- **[CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03932)**  `arXiv:2611.03932`  
  _Robert J. Wang, Charles Ling, Boyu Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

  </details>

- **[RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03850)**  `arXiv:2611.03850`  
  _Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou, Hongru Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating embodied-AI policies in closed loop across simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboTwin requires repeated integration, as each benchmark defines its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention. Evaluation can also be slow: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the 5,000 episodes of RoboTwin Easy take 17.5 hours on four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluators identifies two bottlenecks: alternating between one simulator and inference leaves the GPU at only 14.3% average utilization on LIBERO-Long, while rendering at every control step on RoboTwin means an action-chunk policy reads only one of every 16 rendered observations. We present RoboScope Kit, an evaluation toolkit that integrates each model and benchmark once through a unified interface, keeping each benchmark's native evaluator and scoring, and accelerates evaluation through two mechanisms. (1) Scheduling: simulator workers and policy replicas scale independently, with autotuning sizing both pools to each workload and host. (2) Runtime optimization: the simulation runtime skips unconsumed simulation and rendering work without changing the policy's inputs or outcomes. On a single RTX 4090, RoboScope Kit runs LIBERO-Long 6.2$\times$ faster and 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes 13.2$\times$ faster than StarVLA, and 2.1-7.3$\times$ faster than RLinf and vla-eval. Scaling to four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it evaluates all 5,000 RoboTwin Easy episodes in 66 minutes (15.8$\times$ faster).   </details>

- **[Positive Safety Margins from Artificial Potential Field Reward Augmentation for Size-Robust Obstacle Avoidance under Partial Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02947)**  `arXiv:2611.02947`  
  _Ziyi Hao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.
  </details>

- **[When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41857)**  `arXiv:2610.41857`  
  _Alex Zhou, Junhao Wu, Xueyang Zhou, Yixiao Huo, Hongcheng Gao, Di Zhu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Testing over ten vision language action and world action models on five benchmarks, we find that failures in which the policy has placed the object and the simulator then throws it out are frequent, and that the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa, RoboDojo and RoboLab. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one solver parameter changed. With it we trace each such episode to a false contact. A fixed threshold in PhysX's collision detection makes the engine report an overlap of about two centimeters between the placed object and the thin wall of its container, where the two do not touch. The solver removes the whole overlap in one step and throws the object out at several meters per second. With a smaller threshold, LingBot-VA succeeds in 98 of 100 new episodes against 89, and no episode has an artifact. Across five models, the ranking in the repaired engine follows the ranking on a real robot. SimuGuard also finds two other simulation errors: objects that start inside their support, and objects stuck to an open gripper. SimuGuard lets a benchmark separate what the policy did from what the solver did.
  </details>

- **[MyoAcross: A Framework for Scalable Individualized Musculoskeletal Simulation with a Generalist Morphology-Conditioned Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36535)**  `arXiv:2610.36535`  
  _Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Musculoskeletal simulations powered by deep reinforcement learning (DRL) support human-robot interaction design and rehabilitation engineering, and they typically rely on a generic template model. However, differences in skeletal proportions and body mass alter dynamics, limiting the fidelity of generic models and the reuse of policies trained on them. Scaling individualized simulations requires a framework that connects model construction from accessible inputs with a generalist policy that transfers without fine-tuning. We present MyoAcross, which integrates skeletal-guided individual model construction, generalist morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation for full-body muscle-driven control. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion with a 53.70 mm tracking error, compared with 8.32% completion for a baseline policy trained only on the generic model. Ablation studies show that morphology conditioning improves tracking accuracy while virtual model augmentation broadens generalization. Across input modalities, the pretrained policy demonstrates generalizability to models constructed from body shape (paired with mass), monocular images (paired with height and mass), and marker-based motion capture (paired with mass), making MyoAcross scalable. For biomechanical assessment, MyoAcross improves agreement with measured ground reaction forces and surface electromyography over the generic model on the external Gait120 dataset. These results establish MyoAcross as a practical framework for scalable individualized musculoskeletal simulation. It is suited for systematic cross-individual applications, such as exoskeleton DRL assistance policy design.
  </details>

- **[From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28164)**  `arXiv:2610.28164`  
  _Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25600)**  `arXiv:2610.25600`  
  _Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.
  </details>

- **[Safe Task Completion via Graph-Based Planning for LLM-Powered Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24603)**  `arXiv:2610.24603`  
  _Ali Taheri, Alireza Taban, Qizhou Wang, Wanhua Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to drive robotic manipulation and planning, yet deploying them on physical systems exposes risks, including jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mostly evaluated on short instructions with a single hazard. Real tasks may mix safe and unsafe sub-tasks, or combine individually safe actions into an unsafe outcome. For such compound instructions, a single safety decision either misses the hazard or rejects the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-powered robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules framework that verifies safety at multiple stages rather than relying on a single one. Five agents ground safety principles into world-specific rules, judge each sub-task in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is organized as a graph in which each node handles its assigned rules. Candidate plans are verified and aggregated level by level until one plan satisfies every rule. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions from two benchmarks, measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reaches 0% ASR on both benchmarks and highest TSR among all methods, with 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 83.51% on our long-horizon compound instructions.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21522)**  `arXiv:2610.21522`  
  _Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
  </details>

- **[LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12368)**  `arXiv:2610.12368`  
  _Linkai Liu, Yuntian Zhang, Zhenshan Bing, Chen Chen, Lingjuan Lyu, Shangguang Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences. Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates. We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons, while a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories. In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00-fold end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090. These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.
  </details>

- **[From Language to Motion: Task-Conditioned Focal-Stack Trajectory Integration for Microscopic Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12241)**  `arXiv:2610.12241`  
  _Junjie Xie, Chuxuan He, Junkai Huang, Heng Zhang, Angen Ye, Yujia Song, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Microscopic visual servoing requires a robot to follow fine geometric features that a single image may reveal only in part. At high magnification, the field of view is limited, and shallow depth of field can leave different sections of the same contour sharp at different focal settings. These constraints also make training data costly to annotate, particularly when a change in part or task calls for a different edge, boundary, or offset path. We present a language-guided framework that addresses both the cost of configuring new tasks and the loss of usable geometry in any single focal plane. A language instruction specifies the geometry to recover, while frozen perception models and geometric operators locate it in the images. This separation enables zero-shot reconfiguration for the evaluated tasks without new task-specific training labels. To recover a path across focal planes, we extract local trajectories first and then select a consistent path from the segments supported by the image evidence. Each focal plane can thus contribute the sections it resolves well. The evaluated configuration took 15 minutes. Across nine part and illumination conditions, trajectory-level integration reduced 2-D contour RMSE by 56.4% relative to image-first fusion with SAMFF. In robot dispensing experiments, target-region coverage increased from 83.5% to 92.9%.
  </details>

- **[Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04916)**  `arXiv:2610.04916`  
  _Jing Xie, Shouwei Ruan, Yubin Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Junwei Yang, Songchang Jin, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
  </details>

- **[NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39000)**  `arXiv:2609.39000`  
  _Xiangyu Miao, Junsong Wu, Jiyuan Shi, Weiji Xie, Jinrui Han, Xingyi Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22983)**  `arXiv:2609.22983`  
  _Maksim A Kazanskii_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in SE(3) and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.
  </details>

- **[CHOREO: From Single Skill to Continuous Humanoid Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22274)**  `arXiv:2609.22274`  
  _Ziyi Sun, Jingwen Chen, Yuxi Wang, Xiuze Xia, Long Cheng, Zhaoxiang Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Motion data, RL policies, and generative models give humanoids thousands of skills, and the best general trackers execute nearly all of them alone. Chained to follow a language instruction, the skills fail far more often: in simulation, even the best of eight trackers reaches only 84.9\% sequence success, and their average is 48.9\%. This is because validating a skill alone certifies it only for the tracker that ran it and the state it started from, whereas a sequence keeps one tracker and starts each skill wherever the last one ended. Prior work meets these two conditions mostly by training; CHOREO restores them without retraining by treating every skill as a trajectory that any tracker can run. It assigns each instruction the most precise of its best-validated frozen trackers, which ends each skill closer to the next one's start. It then builds each transition from the measured robot state, escalating to bridges and standing only when needed. On 400 instructions, CHOREO lifts sequence success to 95.8\% and beats always standing between skills by 2.8 points with 42\% shorter transitions. On a physical Unitree G1, all 45 zero-shot trials of nine five-action instructions succeed.
  </details>

- **[WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20892)**  `arXiv:2609.20892`  
  _Guanzhong Sun, Junyi Ma, Yixuan Zhou, Yuxuan Wu, Yanzi Miao, Hesheng Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.
  </details>

- **[Video2Track: Steerable Adversarial Scenario Generation from Real-World Interaction Videos to Proving Grounds for Automated Driving System Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11592)**  `arXiv:2608.11592`  
  _Mengjie Tian, Xinrui Zhang, Tianyu Li, Peizhi Zhang, Guirong Zhuo, Haojie Feng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
